articles.title: Anchorage police and Assembly members clash over technology and surveillance tools
articles.description: Anchorage police and Assembly members clash over technology and surveillance tools Anchorage Daily News
articles.description_html: Anchorage police and Assembly members clash over technology and surveillance tools  Anchorage Daily News
articles.article_title: Anchorage police and Assembly members clash over technology and surveillance tools
articles.heading: Anchorage police and Assembly members clash over technology and surveillance tools
articles.summary: While there are no Flock cameras in Alaska, residents are pushing for checks on police policies.
articles.content:
A dispute over emerging surveillance technology between the Anchorage Police Department and some members of the city’s Assembly will play out Tuesday night during the body’s regular meeting.
On the agenda are two distinct, but overlapping, items that have come up as flashpoints amid public concerns about how new technologies are being adopted by law enforcement agencies in Anchorage and across the country.
“Amid a nationwide backlash to surveillance systems like Flock and Axon, the mayor of Anchorage has doubled down on the establishment of her own system here at home,” said South Anchorage Assembly member Keith McCormick in a video posted to social media over the weekend, referring to two technology companies that contract with police departments.
The measure would expand restrictions on technology laid out in municipal code, and curb the police department’s ability to guide and implement many of its own policies when it comes to emergent surveillance tools.
“Code in and of itself is not going to be able to keep up with how agile a police department needs to be in a modern world to be able to remotely keep up with crime. It just won’t,” APD Chief Sean Case said during testimony at an Assembly work session on Aug. 21.
That surveillance measure is up for public testimony before the Assembly on Tuesday evening, after which point members may discuss it further, vote on it or send it off for further refinement.
The same agenda also includes a request from the police department and Mayor Suzanne LaFrance to approve nearly $600,000 in support of the Real Time Crime Center, a hub for consolidating various streams of information during criminal investigations like kidnappings, vehicle pursuits and assaults as they occur. That money would purchase hardware and equipment for work Anchorage police are already doing. This funding request faces some Assembly pushback over the department’s broader use of technology.
“APD leadership currently, Chief Case especially with how he addressed the Assembly during the work session, gives me great pause in giving them additional resources for that,” McCormick said in an interview Monday.
APD surveillance technology
In the national discourse around surveillance, one company brought up more than most is Flock. At its core, the Georgia-based company sells customers cameras that read car license plates. The cameras are networked, so they can feed in reams of data and video footage that can be potentially stored indefinitely. Purchasing entities like police departments, municipal governments or homeowners associations have a range of options for what they do with that data. According to reporting by the New York Times, there are around 120,000 Flock cameras spread over every state in the country except one: Alaska.
“Right now, we don’t have Flock safety cameras in the state of Alaska,” Case told the Assembly during its August work session.
Data from DeFlock, an open-source project tracking automated license plate readers around the country, does not show any such mounted cameras in Alaska.
But the Anchorage Police Department does draw on a number of similar technologies and capabilities, and is generally very proactive about adopting new tools, Case said in an interview last week.
“We’re just trying to enhance what the officer can do,” Case said, adding that one of his goals is for the department to be a leader in intelligently and effectively implementing new technology systems to its policing.
Many of the tools and technologies picked up by APD in the last several years — with the approval of body cameras by voters and elected leaders — do not add new capabilities, Case said, but help officers, detectives, dispatchers and others do their same work faster.
APD patrol cruisers have the ability to read license plates in real time, he said. While Flock cameras are mounted in place and take video of each car that passes, APD vehicle dash cams have a software component purchased through the company Axon that read any license plate in their field of view. Artificial intelligence deciphers the plate numbers and automatically runs it against databases to check for stolen vehicles or felony connections. If there’s a “hit” on a plate near a police cruiser and a database entry, the system alerts the officer, who then has to confirm there’s not an error and decide how to proceed.
[From 2025: Anchorage police unveil plans to use license plate readers, array of security cameras]
This, Case said, is very similar to how officers have long checked whether a vehicle might be involved in a crime — only in the past, they did it by using their eyes, punching digits into their computers, then waiting for results. Now, the automated license plate reader does it for them.
“The use of technology is just completely compressing that timeframe,” Case said.
Detectives in the department are using artificial intelligence systems similar to commercial large language models like ChatGPT and Gemini Notebook to manage case files and query them more efficiently, Case said.
The Real Time Crime Center fits a similar paradigm. The “center” itself is not much more than a windowless office in the depths of APD’s old building with a few desks, computers and a large overhead monitor. One to two trained officers overseen by a commander take information from dispatchers, patrol units, public records, databases and live video feeds from city-owned traffic cameras to intervene in active crimes or rapidly begin investigating them.
While the technology package purchased through Axon could potentially accommodate as many as 750 different feeds coming in at one time, the Anchorage Police Department has neither the hardware nor personnel to come anywhere close to that, Case said. Most of what the Real Time Crime Center does is expedite existing police work, not expand it into new capacities or domains, Case said.
“Really, what we’ve done is we’ve added technology so that we can pull all of our video feeds together,” he said.
The $598,998 requested for the Real Time Crime Center, funded through federal asset forfeitures, would pay for the audio-visual equipment to make the facilities more functional, according to a memorandum submitted to the Assembly in support of the measure. That includes more monitors, office furniture, control boards and similar hardware.
A number of businesses in Anchorage, particularly big box retailers, have also started sharing data among themselves and with APD on shoplifting through a platform called Auror. In May, the department and mayor’s office credited the program with enabling a high degree of cooperation among merchants and law enforcement that has helped build bigger theft cases against repeat offenders and issue charges more quickly.
[Anchorage police say public safety efforts have led to hundreds of shoplifting charges]
Code first, tech second
A lot of what’s at issue in the schism between Assembly members and APD comes down to whether guardrails on surveillance technologies ought to be spelled out in police policies or written in code.
The police department puts many of its official policies and procedures online for the public to access, including its rules for automatic license plate readers, the Real Time Crime Center and other sensitive topics. But those policies can change depending on the priorities of a chief or political leaders.
Municipal code is law, which is firmer but also much slower and harder to change.
“Code is not going to keep up with technology,” Case told the Assembly in August.
McCormick, who often takes conservative positions on issues, has partnered on a technology ordinance with two of the Assembly’s more liberal-leaning members, Vice Chair Daniel Volland and Sydney Scout, both of whom represent downtown Anchorage.
Volland, one of the new technology ordinance’s sponsors, thinks public process should precede technological adoption.
“I find that disturbing. I don’t think we need to be putting the cart before the horse when it comes to potentially sacrificing people’s privacy rights,” Volland said.
He said the ordinance was not drafted in response to any excesses or abuse by APD. The current section of code dealing with surveillance technologies, passed in 2023, takes some of the rules currently written in police policy — like deleting digital records after 14 days unless entered as evidence in a case — and adds them to the municipal rulebook.
“For me this is about taking a proactive approach,” Volland said.
In its current form, the measure affects APD’s ability to use money for technology purchases.
“Regardless of the amount involved, all contracts for the procurement of surveillance technology or services ... must be approved in advance by the Assembly,” the ordinance states.
Mike Garvey, policy director for the American Civil Liberties Union of Alaska, said the group supports the Assembly proposal to add more surveillance and technology restrictions through the code overhaul.
“Laws have more permanence and are more resistant to change,” Garvey said Monday.
Case said many of APD’s policies and procedures on surveillance are already more restrictive than those of police peers in the Lower 48, largely because of Alaska’s robust privacy protections. The department has taken an incremental approach to bringing new procedures online, he said, to give the public and officials more time to react. Any policy has to strike a balance between speed and efficacy on the one hand, along with privacy and civil liberties protections on the other, Case said.
Volland said that after public testimony on the expanded code provisions, he anticipates the ordinance will continue to be refined by the Assembly, and that he would like the Real Time Crime Center funding measure to follow a similar timeline before it gets a vote.
The Assembly meets Tuesday evening for its regular meeting beginning at 5 p.m. in its chambers at the Loussac Library and streamed live online.

articles.article_title: Technological Change Requires Constant Learning
articles.heading: Technological Change Requires Constant Learning
articles.summary: Technological Change Requires Constant Learning
articles.content:
NDIA PERSPECTIVE EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES
Technological Change Requires Constant Learning
By William “Mac" Thornberry
NDIA photo
I suspect I am not alone in being amazed and sometimes a little overwhelmed by all of the changes going on around us. It is not just how much things are changing; it is how fast those changes are taking place.
The pace of technological change in particular has enormous implications for the U.S. economy, for how we receive and process information, and for many aspects of our daily life. It also has implications for the nation’s security.
In recent weeks, we have read about unmanned vehicles rescuing U.S. servicemembers at sea, Ukraine regaining territory using unmanned ground vehicles and some AI models considered too powerful for release while others break out of their test environment. And that is just a sampling.
Technological change brings a number of challenges with it. We have more information at our fingertips than any people in the history of the world, yet it is harder than ever to know what is true and harder still to put what we think to be true in context — to understand what it means, how it relates to other changes, what lessons from the past might apply and what the future may hold.
Of course, we also have to sort through the ethical and moral issues raised by some of these technologies. Again, warfare is no exception.
More than a few times I have heard the comment that the biggest obstacle in protecting U.S. national security is not developing new technology, it is the humans who interact with that technology. History is certainly full of examples when acceptance of breakthroughs has lagged, not to mention the organization, doctrine and training required to take full advantage of them.
Change is always hard for those on top. There are times when businesses are required to upend the very things that made them successful in order to remain competitive. That dilemma can apply to nations as well.
What all of this adds up to, in my mind, is that more is required of national security leaders in and out of government than ever before. We all have an obligation to constantly be learning and to dig under the headlines to consider which changes truly matter and what the consequences might be.
However powerful it may be, we cannot outsource our thinking or our judgment to AI. But thinking requires effort, and we must be intentional about it.
Henry Ford, in a 1928 interview about pace and complexity of change, said: “But there is a question in my mind whether, with all this speeding up of our everyday activities, there is any more real thinking. Thinking is the hardest work there is, which is the probable reason why so few engage in it.”
As the leader among defense and national security associations, the National Defense Industrial Association recognized the challenges posed by rapid technological change and in 2021 launched the Emerging Technologies Institute to help educate, enlighten and adapt to technological changes and their implications for national security.
ETI conducts cutting-edge research and analysis, producing reports, tutorials and podcasts — all to help a variety of audiences understand and make sense of the swirl of developments around us.
The institute also spurs collaboration, partnering with a variety of government and non-government groups to explore and advance new technologies and their applications for national security. It delves even deeper into supply chains, advanced materials and manufacturing, and technology adoption, focusing on best practices.
ETI’s flagship event, the fourth annual Emerging Technologies for Defense Conference and Exhibition, will be held in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 8 through 10. It will feature prominent national security leaders, row after row of exhibits and countless opportunities for informal connections and interactions.
Whatever our background and experience, I guarantee that there are new things to learn — and best of all, we will all have the opportunity to engage in the hard work of thinking.
William “Mac” Thornberry is the chair of the Emerging Technologies Institute Advisory Board and former chairman of the House Armed Services Committee.
Topics: Defense Innovation, Defense Department

The institute also spurs collaboration, partnering with a variety of government and non-government groups to explore and advance new technologies and their applications for national security. It delves even deeper into supply chains, advanced materials and manufacturing, and technology adoption, focusing on best practices.

ETI’s flagship event, the fourth annual Emerging Technologies for Defense Conference and Exhibition, will be held in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 8 through 10. It will feature prominent national security leaders, row after row of exhibits and countless opportunities for informal connections and interactions.

Whatever our background and experience, I guarantee that there are new things to learn — and best of all, we will all have the opportunity to engage in the hard work of thinking.

William “Mac” Thornberry is the chair of the Emerging Technologies Institute Advisory Board and former chairman of the House Armed Services Committee.

articles.title: "Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology
articles.description: "Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology Hyperallergic
articles.description_html: "Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology  Hyperallergic
articles.article_title: "Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology
articles.heading: "Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology
articles.summary: Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez's new performance is a grotesque parade of visual delights that defangs our toxic relationship to our screens.
articles.content:
"Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology
Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez's new performance is a grotesque parade of visual delights that defangs our toxic relationship to our screens.
Artistic attempts to contend with technology’s ever-tightening grip on our attention, institutions, and social abilities too often take the form of post-human fever dreams of the Black Mirror school — works that, while intended to be critical, devolve into discursive, cyborg-filled feedback loops. Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez’s Marina, which premiered at Manhattan’s Little Island last week as part of the 2026 Whitney Biennial program, opts for a radically different tack: laughing at technology instead of fearing it and winning our hearts rather than rotting our brains.
The air is humid with a storm that never materialized as audience members stream into The Amph, Little Island’s open-air amphitheater, on Thursday, August 26. Onstage, a figure in a burgundy pinstripe suit mouths wordlessly into a payphone set on a wooden dock suspended above a vaguely apocalyptic underwater mise-en-scène. Framed video screens playing water-wave patterns rise from coral outcroppings encrusted with rubber-tire bits, junk, and debris.
Down in the murky waters of the Gowanus Canal, we learn, reside a sea wench named Marina (played by Gutierrez), her overprotective older sister, and an anglerfish named Nano. They lead a parasitic existence, accruing the trash that sinks to the floor to reinforce their shells. No one seems to question their sedentary lifestyle until a distracted construction worker, barking his insecurities to his AI girlfriend while pacing the dock above them, drops his smartphone into the water. (“Is this a rectangle?” Nano asks, unironically.) Entrances by the device, Marina is drawn into a world of endless scrolls and highlight reels, where influencers peddle the familiar doctrine that a woman can find self-worth only through a man's validation. If this is all sounding very truth-universally-acknowledged so far, that’s because the plot of Marina is Frankensteined from paradigmatic tales of women scorned, from Homer’s Odyssey to Euripides’s Medea to Jennifer’s Body (2009).
Our protagonist sets out with good intentions at first, snapping a candid selfie atop her garbage pile and uploading it to OkCupid, a platform that feels as dated a reference as the payphone. But no one swipes right, so she does what we all do online, to some degree or another: She pretends to be someone else. Marina finds her perfect alter-ego in a more conventionally attractive sea dweller, Ariel of Disney’s The Little Mermaid (1989), whose wide eyes and frizz-free red mane lure thirsty suitors like Jared, a “man of faith” who swears he’s 6’5 and a CEO but “will not be tasked with the emotional labor of dealing with your trauma.” In other words, they are not exactly a catch. When they realize they’ve quite literally been catfished and grow aggressive, they face the homicidal ire of Marina, their Apple Watches and motorcycle jackets becoming absorbed into her ever-growing junkyard ecology.
Back on terra firma, our pinstriped narrator, a detective perennially attached to a payphone, is determined to crack the case of the fuckboys going missing down below. She recruits a randy garbageman named Dino to go undercover (“I’ll make it worth your while, but not by a lot — I’m solving this case on spec.”) But as the saying goes, there’s a lid for every pot, and Marina is just Dino’s type: large claws, “kinky,” no interest in deodorant. Marina must now confront the greatest challenge of becoming oneself: learning to locate a sense of identity in her own existence.

articles.title: OPINION: Get technology out of college classrooms
articles.description: OPINION: Get technology out of college classrooms Indiana Daily Student
articles.description_html: OPINION: Get technology out of college classrooms  Indiana Daily Student
articles.source: OPINION: Get technology out of college classrooms  - Indiana Daily Student
articles.article_title: OPINION: Get technology out of college classrooms
articles.heading: OPINION: Get technology out of college classrooms
articles.summary: Ill-equipped for higher education, students could benefit from analog courses.
articles.content:
It’s a time of experimentation in higher education. That’s a tell that something is wrong.
As your high school science teacher drilled, the first step in the scientific method is noticing a problem. In this case: Why are college-bound students, despite increasing high-school GPAs — and a record-high graduation rate — less prepared for college-level coursework than ever before?
Among first-semester Calculus I students at the University of California, Berkeley, a third displayed “severe preparation deficits” between 2020–23. In franker speak, one in three high school students in that period didn’t graduate with high-school level skills. That trend continues. And so, in July, over 2,300 STEM faculty in the UC system signed a letter asking that the university reinstate SAT/ACT score requirements for STEM-focused applicants.
The second step is offering a hypothesis: Something is not working in K–12 education.
State legislatures connect declining learning outcomes with the ubiquity of phones: 26, including Indiana’s, have banned the use of phones during the academic day. And why not? Over the last decade, dwindling test scores have coincided with the proliferation of smart phones among Americans. But the link is, at best, dubious.
Besides student well-being — a wonderfully vague term — researchers at Stanford University, studying data of 43,000 schools, did not find increased test scores, or many other benefits of phone-free schooling.
Surely, a broader range of factors contribute to the present crisis in learning, not reduceable to a single, conveniently visible scapegoat. It can't help that parents do too little to hold their kids academically accountable, at least according to teachers. But it also can’t help that two-thirds of teens get distracted by digital devices during the school day. Distracted students, presumably, perform worse on tests.
Basing policy on common sentiment — vibes, if you like — that contradicts critical research probably worsens problems more often than not. See tariffs, for example. Vibes might tell us that American manufacturing is suffering and needs the strong arm of the government to protect it. Economic data, however, shows that heavy industry in the United States is more productive, and stronger, than ever. Meanwhile, tariffs wreak pocketbook havoc.
But something is wrong in K–12 education, and that dysfunction creeps into higher education every time a high school senior graduates. So, universities must try something. Much like their students, some are experimenting in 1960s-style free-spiritism:
At the University of Michigan, the College of Literature, Science and Arts will hide first-semester grades from transcripts beginning in fall 2027, with the goal of “allow(ing) intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys.”
When second semester comes, Michigan surmises, un-ready college students whose incentives to become ready have been stripped, will, through “intrinsic motivation,” be suddenly transformed into ready students. Michigan offers no suggestion as to where that intrinsic motivation will arise from.
Because Michigan's experiment is doubtful to pan out, universities might as well try solutions a tad more conservative — more rule-bound, rigid "1950s-style."
In the same timeframe as Michigan, the College of the University of Chicago will ban the use of technology in certain general education classes. Chicago supposes that increasing, not lowering, expectations will profit students' study ethic.
A simple test as to which of these experiments will prove more beneficial is to ask which the unmotivated student would prefer? Obviously, the hidden grade policy. After determining that, opt for the other experiment. Expecting more of students — to participate more fully in class — through extrinsic pushes like technology bans is a better bet.
There is still time for the College of Arts and Sciences at Indiana University to adopt such a policy ahead of the 2027 academic year. The college should stand behind professors who already restrict the usage of screens in their courses and encourage others to do so as well, especially in first- and second-year classes where screens are not integral to the subject.
Admittedly, technology is good. If Ned Ludd had had his druthers, the world would be worse off. Technology increases productivity while diminishing the human toil required. It’s useful at making more things more easily and, on a collective scale, is the reason why many can delay entry into the workforce, say, four years to obtain a bachelor’s degree.
But exactly the effortlessness that technology offers is counterproductive when the goal is not output but resistance — mental or physical. Arguments that technology in the classroom is necessary to prepare students for the technology they’ll encounter in the workforce amount to arguments against hitting the gym in a world where forklifts instead of manpower move boxes in warehouses. Of course, the latter argument is absurd. Outsourcing manpower enfeebles muscle; outsourcing brainpower erodes gray cells.
In my last column, I predicted a smaller future for higher education. Not only are there fewer students because of declining birth rates. The economic depreciation of college degrees means of these fewer students, fewer will choose college. As a result, many institutions of higher education will be shutting their doors over the next decades.
Academia's smaller future could resemble their equally small past, where it was a place of leisure rather than a license to work. In such a future, where academic pursuits are increasingly sought for their own sake, the students who choose college will likely want something different than high school, something challenging, which will engage them in intellectually strenuous activities.
Universities can prepare for this future now by following the example that Chicago’s College has set.
Eric Cannon (he/him) is a junior studying philosophy and political science and currently serves as a member of IU Student Government. Never miss his columns or other opinionated musings on X.

Vibes might tell us that American manufacturing is suffering and needs the strong arm of the government to protect it. Economic data, however, shows that heavy industry in the United States is more productive, and stronger, than ever. Meanwhile, tariffs wreak pocketbook havoc.

But something is wrong in K–12 education, and that dysfunction creeps into higher education every time a high school senior graduates. So, universities must try something. Much like their students, some are experimenting in 1960s-style free-spiritism:

At the University of Michigan, the College of Literature, Science and Arts will hide first-semester grades from transcripts beginning in fall 2027, with the goal of “allow(ing) intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys.”

When second semester comes, Michigan surmises, un-ready college students whose incentives to become ready have been stripped, will, through “intrinsic motivation,” be suddenly transformed into ready students. Michigan offers no suggestion as to where that intrinsic motivation will arise from.

Because Michigan's experiment is doubtful to pan out, universities might as well try solutions a tad more conservative — more rule-bound, rigid "1950s-style."

In the same timeframe as Michigan, the College of the University of Chicago will ban the use of technology in certain general education classes. Chicago supposes that increasing, not lowering, expectations will profit students' study ethic.

A simple test as to which of these experiments will prove more beneficial is to ask which the unmotivated student would prefer? Obviously, the hidden grade policy. After determining that, opt for the other experiment. Expecting more of students — to participate more fully in class — through extrinsic pushes like technology bans is a better bet.

There is still time for the College of Arts and Sciences at Indiana University to adopt such a policy ahead of the 2027 academic year. The college should stand behind professors who already restrict the usage of screens in their courses and encourage others to do so as well, especially in first- and second-year classes where screens are not integral to the subject.

Admittedly, technology is good. If Ned Ludd had had his druthers, the world would be worse off. Technology increases productivity while diminishing the human toil required. It’s useful at making more things more easily and, on a collective scale, is the reason why many can delay entry into the workforce, say, four years to obtain a bachelor’s degree.

But exactly the effortlessness that technology offers is counterproductive when the goal is not output but resistance — mental or physical. Arguments that technology in the classroom is necessary to prepare students for the technology they’ll encounter in the workforce amount to arguments against hitting the gym in a world where forklifts instead of manpower move boxes in warehouses. Of course, the latter argument is absurd. Outsourcing manpower enfeebles muscle; outsourcing brainpower erodes gray cells.

In my last column, I predicted a smaller future for higher education. Not only are there fewer students because of declining birth rates. The economic depreciation of college degrees means of these fewer students, fewer will choose college. As a result, many institutions of higher education will be shutting their doors over the next decades.

Academia's smaller future could resemble their equally small past, where it was a place of leisure rather than a license to work. In such a future, where academic pursuits are increasingly sought for their own sake, the students who choose college will likely want something different than high school, something challenging, which will engage them in intellectually strenuous activities.

Universities can prepare for this future now by following the example that Chicago’s College has set.

Eric Cannon (he/him) is a junior studying philosophy and political science and currently serves as a member of IU Student Government. Never miss his columns or other opinionated musings on X.

articles.content:
WOOD DALE, Ill., Aug. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AAR CORP. (NYSE: AIR), the leading parts, repair, and software platform in the aviation aftermarket, announced that Sanjay Sood joined the Company as Senior Vice President and Chief Digital & Technology Officer, effective today.
Sood will oversee AAR's technology organization, including enterprise systems, infrastructure, cybersecurity, data and analytics, and the Company's efforts to further leverage AI and other technologies across its operations. He will report to John M. Holmes, Chairman, President and CEO.
Most recently, Sood served as Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer at CDW, a leading multi-brand provider of information technology solutions, where he modernized the company's platforms, data architecture, and AI initiatives and managed the technical integration of multiple acquisitions. Prior to CDW, Sood held senior technology and product leadership positions at HERE Technologies, where he was responsible for global engineering organizations and building emerging products. Earlier in his career, he held leadership roles at YP, formerly AT&T Interactive, AllVoices, and BuzzLabs.
Sood earned a Ph.D. in Computer Science and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science and Communication Studies from Northwestern University.
"Sanjay brings a unique combination of significant experience in large-scale information technology leadership, infrastructure modernization, and AI technology implementation," said Holmes. "We are pleased to welcome Sanjay to the AAR team. His leadership will be critical as we continue executing our long-term strategy and strengthening the systems and data management that help our business operate effectively."
"I look forward to helping connect information across the organization, build on the strong foundation already in place, and reinforce the operational discipline that has long defined AAR," said Sood. "Advancing AAR's vast data resources is key to driving further value and efficiency for customers."
For more information on AAR, visit aarcorp.com.
About AAR
AAR is a leading global aerospace and defense aftermarket solutions company with operations in over 20 countries. Headquartered in the Chicago area, AAR supports commercial and government customers through three primary operating segments: Parts Supply; Repair, Engineering, and Software; and Government Solutions. Additional information can be found at aarcorp.com.

articles.title: Meet Scooby: S.C. K9 helps find hidden technology to protect kids
articles.description: Meet Scooby: S.C. K9 helps find hidden technology to protect kids WRDW
articles.description_html: Meet Scooby: S.C. K9 helps find hidden technology to protect kids  WRDW
articles.article_title: Meet Scooby: S.C. K9 helps find hidden technology to protect kids
articles.heading: Meet Scooby: S.C. K9 helps find hidden technology to protect kids
articles.summary: K9 Scooby is one of the many resources the department’s Internet Crimes Against Children division deploys in investigations.
articles.content:
Meet Scooby: S.C. K9 helps find hidden technology to protect kids
GREENVILLE, S.C. - Meet Scooby, a golden retriever that works in electronic detection with the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office.
Don’t be fooled by his cuteness - this K9 does serious work to help protect children from abuse.
K9 Scooby is one of the many resources the department’s Internet Crimes Against Children division deploys in investigations.
Body of missing 5-year-old girl recovered in South Carolina
The body of a nonverbal 5-year-old girl who went missing has been recovered in Pawleys Island, South Carolina.
Scooby’s handler, Investigator Alicia Turner, said the division receives about 40 cyber tips a month, which originate when tech platforms such as Google or Facebook detect potential child exploitation material via automated hashing and AI algorithms. These are flagged to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which routes them to local law enforcement.
Turner explained that Scooby is trained to detect triphenylphosphine oxide, a chemical coating applied to electronic components to prevent overheating.
While human eyes can easily miss micro SD cards, flash drives, or carefully hidden “ghost” cellphones, Scooby’s sense of smell can recover devices that may be hidden. In exchange for successful finds, the food-reward-trained Scooby gets a snack.
Aiken community honors Javeayah Harris with memorial service
The CSRA came together for a memorial service to remember Javeayah Harris on Sunday afternoon.
“All he’s looking for is that odor, and he wants to find that odor because he wants to get food,” Turner shared.
Turner shared that the Greenville County Sheriff’s Office ICAC unit is one of the largest in the Southeast.
“That comes from the top. It comes from a sheriff that cares about children and the children in our county,” Turner said. “There are sheriffs that absolutely refuse to work these types of cases, and they say it’s the attorney general office’s job. That’s not okay because that just puts more on their plate, and that’s fewer children we can save.”
Safety reminders
Turner shared that in the digital age, parents can’t protect children enough. She cautions parents from even giving their child cellphone access.
“Would you go to Times Square in New York and just let your 10-year-old roam and let everybody have contact with her? No. But when you give them this cellphone, you’re giving the world contact to your child. These offenders and pedophiles, they’re on the kids’ apps. Any kids’ app that has a chat is going to have a bad guy.”
Parents are also reminded of the following:
- Implement random passcode checks on children’s devices.
- Watch for “ghost apps,” or chat platforms that are disguised as calculators on devices.
- Do not hand over smartphones to young children without strict boundaries.
- Utilize resources from NCMEC to facilitate age-appropriate digital safety conversations.

articles.title: Ball State University Receives EAB Technology Pioneer Award for Innovation in Student Success
articles.description: Ball State University Receives EAB Technology Pioneer Award for Innovation in Student Success Ball State University
articles.description_html: Ball State University Receives EAB Technology Pioneer Award for Innovation in Student Success  Ball State University
articles.article_title: Ball State University Receives EAB Technology Pioneer Award for Innovation in Student Success
articles.heading: Ball State University Receives EAB Technology Pioneer Award for Innovation in Student Success
articles.summary: Ball State University has been named the recipient of EAB’s 2026 Technology Pioneer Award, recognizing the University’s innovative use of technology to strengthen student success and provide more coordinated, proactive support for students.
articles.content:
Ball State University has been named the recipient of EAB’s 2026 Technology Pioneer Award, recognizing the University’s innovative use of technology to strengthen student success and provide more coordinated, proactive support for students.
The Technology Pioneer Award recognizes institutions that are leading the way in their use of EAB technology, including those that implement new tools or use existing platforms in innovative ways. EAB selected Ball State in particular for its integration of EAB Navigate360 with Canvas, the University’s learning management system, as well as its broader, evolving approach to using Navigate360 to advance student success.
“Technology can tell us a great deal about where a student may be struggling, but the real value comes from what we do with that information,” said Dr. Jason Rivera, vice provost for student success and dean of University College. “Our approach to student success is grounded in a simple idea: students are more likely to thrive when they are connected to people who know them, care about their progress, and can help them navigate challenges. What has made the difference at Ball State is the way faculty, advisors, student success professionals, and technology partners have worked together to make those connections happen.”
Ball State began implementing Navigate360 in Spring 2022, with full implementation that Fall. Since then, the University has steadily expanded use of the platform as part of a coordinated student-support network involving faculty, academic advisors, student success professionals, Information Technology staff, and other campus partners.
Among those efforts, Ball State has developed a coordinated schedule of alerts and progress-reporting campaigns throughout each semester, giving faculty additional opportunities to identify students who may benefit from academic or other support. The University also uses Navigate360 to collect midterm grades and help coordinate appropriate follow-up.
In Spring 2026, Ball State further enhanced that work through an integration between Navigate360 and Canvas. The integration simplified faculty participation in progress reporting while giving the University a more connected view of students’ academic engagement and progress.
Faculty participation in the Spring 2026 midterm progress-reporting campaign exceeded 90 percent. Faculty submitted approximately 9,600 at-risk progress reports during the semester. Among reports for which both midterm and final grade data were available, 43 percent showed an improved grade by the end of the semester. Among 9,163 progress reports containing letter grades that could be converted to grade-point values, students improved by an average of 0.47 GPA points from midterm to the end of the semester.
“The success of this work has depended on people across Ball State coming together around a common objective: making it easier to support our students,” said Alissa Goldsworthy, project manager and system analyst in Ball State’s Enterprise Project Management Office. “Integrating Navigate360 and Canvas required us to think carefully about how faculty use these systems, how information moves between them, and how we could make that process more useful and efficient. The result is technology that better supports the people doing this work every day and helps the University respond to students in a more timely and coordinated way.”
Ball State’s approach supports priorities outlined in Destination 2040: Our Flight Path, the University’s long-term strategic plan. Among its strategic imperatives, Ball State is committed to engaging faculty and staff in comprehensive student-success strategies that provide a relationship-rich experience for undergraduate students and to strategically aligning people, processes, and technology to support academic excellence and institutional effectiveness.
EAB’s Connected Awards—previously known as the Student Success Collaborative Awards—recognize leaders and institutions advancing student success and institutional goals through thoughtful strategy, collaboration, and effective use of technology.
Ball State will be recognized during CONNECTED26, EAB’s annual conference for higher education leaders, Oct. 26-28 in Orlando, Fla. Dr. Rivera and Ms. Goldsworthy are also expected to share Ball State’s implementation strategy with conference participants, including the University’s integration of Navigate360 and Canvas and its broader approach to coordinated student support.

articles.title: Playing against climate risk
articles.description: Playing against climate risk MIT News
articles.description_html: Playing against climate risk  MIT News
articles.source: MIT News | Massachusetts Institute of Technology
articles.article_title: Playing against climate risk
articles.heading: Playing against climate risk
articles.summary: MIT researchers are helping small coastal communities in India prepare for natural disasters using climate model-based games. The project is led by Sai Ravela, a J-WAFS researcher and principal research scientist in the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences.
articles.content:
Sai Ravela, principal research scientist in MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), works with a team of researchers, local partners, and community collaborators to develop game-based computer models to help local communities find solutions to their unique geographical and environmental challenges.
Ravela came to MIT as a postdoc in 2002. Prior to that, he had been working on robotics and computer vision, but he was excited by the idea of studying the climate system and wanted to work in the field of sustainability. “Suddenly, overnight, I became a climate person,” Ravela says.
His project, funded by a 2025 Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS) India Grant, explores how agricultural decision-making occurs under climate stress. Using localized climate projections and a participatory approach, the project aims to help communities discover ways to improve their collective agricultural resilience.
EAPS postdoc Anamitra Saha is a key contributor on the grant, working with Ravela and local collaborators to combine downscaled climate modeling, participatory decision-making, and community-based adaptation planning. Other team members include Myisha Ahmad (Carthago Consultancy), Jayanta Basu (University of Calcutta), Anusree Ghosh (Bangladesh Open University), Showmitra Sarkar (Khulna University of Engineering and Technology), and Bivuti Sikder (Dhaka University).
In a process known as downscaling, researchers take large-scale climate projections and turn them into highly detailed local projections. From these hazard maps, Ravela and Saha can estimate the risk of extreme weather phenomena such as flooding, drought, heat waves, and salinity-related stress.
“We kind of simulate what the outcome could be in that region,” Ravela explains. “Would it improve agricultural productivity? Would it reduce agricultural productivity? Would it change certain land use patterns? Would the land be less livable, more livable?”
The team combines surveys, scientific models, and local knowledge to build an impact graph that allows them to explore what might happen to a region during simulated weather events.
Although Ravela knew hazard maps could be useful, he was troubled by how rarely they reached the people whose lives were most affected by the risks they described. “We had clients like insurance companies,” he says. “But I never saw it reach people in a way that made a difference in their lives. And that really bothered me.”
To address this gap, he began thinking about how to help communities engage with hazard maps directly and take part in the decision-making process. In conversations that informed the game’s development, Ravela heard people whose livelihoods are vulnerable to climate events voice immediate concerns about what would happen if a future season failed: “If I don’t plant next season — if I can’t — what would I do?” Ravela wanted to help people think instead about possible choices, different paths, and their respective risks.
When he asked himself what circumstances allow someone to think about risk, the answer began to take shape. “Well, roll a die. Toss a coin,” he thought. “And where do you do these things? In a game.”
How it works
The process the collaborating team developed takes place in three stages. The first is a “snakes and ladders” game, played with physical game pieces and tokens. The second is a mixed game that still uses the gameboard, but a computer generates events and manages portfolios, allowing the system to calculate risk percentages. Once players become comfortable with the mixed game, the final stage, developed by Ravela, abandons the board game and moves fully into a more detailed computer simulation that can be played on a cellphone app.
“We tried this in different stages in three places,” says Ravela. Two villages, Bally Island and Joygopalpur, are in India's Sundarbans region. The third is a village in Bangladesh just across the border. In each location, the work depends on collaboration with local residents, community organizers, and regional partners who help shape the game around local land, water, livelihood, and governance conditions. During development, informal community-engagement sessions helped the team refine and adapt the game. Those interactions also led to intriguing observations that are now helping the team formulate hypotheses for future formal research.
The three villages lie in a coastal region that faces numerous extreme weather events threatening water availability and agricultural productivity. As riverbeds rise from sediment accumulation over time and the land sinks from groundwater extraction, saltwater can more easily intrude into groundwater aquifers, while freshwater drainage, recharge, and flushing become increasingly difficult, intensifying waterlogging and drought.
“There’s a vicious cycle that’s happening with salinization of the soil,” Ravela explains.
One visible result is that Boro rice leaves now often begin browning far too early in the season, as salinity and water stress damage crops before they can mature. This cycle occurs in many coastal communities, suggesting to Ravela that the outcomes of the J-WAFS project could have applications around the world.
That broader potential comes from what the game is able to reveal. Instead of treating potential interventions — such as embankments, canals, recharge, crops, fisheries, and energy — as separate choices, the simulation lets players see how each intervention affects the coupled system of land, water, salinity, and livelihoods. When players test different options, simply raising embankments often proves less effective than expected, because it does not break the underlying cycle that causes the land to flood.
More-integrated strategies — combining mangrove restoration, canal excavation, groundwater recharge, diversified agriculture and fisheries, better water management, and merging solar panels into farming with agrivoltaics or aquavoltaics — can generate better long-term returns while also making the landscape more resilient.
The game also creates space to consider dramatic alternatives to embankment-based protection, including seasonal migration, livelihood shifts, and other difficult choices. These possibilities can be explored safely inside the game, even when they would be almost unimaginable to raise in real life. In this way, difficult questions that might otherwise be avoided can be explored, rather than ignored. And if the game reveals that a difficult choice could lead to better long-term outcomes, that result is not a prescription, but a basis for informed conversation between the community, government, and other decision-makers.
Competition or cooperation?
To make the game effective at developing strategies, Ravela’s team had to understand how many people should play at one time. Too few players may not generate enough diversity of ideas, while too many can slow the process significantly. During game development, groups of roughly ten to twelve people seemed especially workable: large enough to support active interaction, but small enough for practical discussion and learning.

Sai Ravela, principal research scientist in MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), works with a team of researchers, local partners, and community collaborators to develop game-based computer models to help local communities find solutions to their unique geographical and environmental challenges.

Ravela came to MIT as a postdoc in 2002. Prior to that, he had been working on robotics and computer vision, but he was excited by the idea of studying the climate system and wanted to work in the field of sustainability. “Suddenly, overnight, I became a climate person,” Ravela says.

His project, funded by a 2025 Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS) India Grant, explores how agricultural decision-making occurs under climate stress. Using localized climate projections and a participatory approach, the project aims to help communities discover ways to improve their collective agricultural resilience.

EAPS postdoc Anamitra Saha is a key contributor on the grant, working with Ravela and local collaborators to combine downscaled climate modeling, participatory decision-making, and community-based adaptation planning. Other team members include Myisha Ahmad (Carthago Consultancy), Jayanta Basu (University of Calcutta), Anusree Ghosh (Bangladesh Open University), Showmitra Sarkar (Khulna University of Engineering and Technology), and Bivuti Sikder (Dhaka University).

In a process known as downscaling, researchers take large-scale climate projections and turn them into highly detailed local projections. From these hazard maps, Ravela and Saha can estimate the risk of extreme weather phenomena such as flooding, drought, heat waves, and salinity-related stress.

“We kind of simulate what the outcome could be in that region,” Ravela explains. “Would it improve agricultural productivity? Would it reduce agricultural productivity? Would it change certain land use patterns? Would the land be less livable, more livable?”

The team combines surveys, scientific models, and local knowledge to build an impact graph that allows them to explore what might happen to a region during simulated weather events.

Although Ravela knew hazard maps could be useful, he was troubled by how rarely they reached the people whose lives were most affected by the risks they described. “We had clients like insurance companies,” he says. “But I never saw it reach people in a way that made a difference in their lives. And that really bothered me.”

To address this gap, he began thinking about how to help communities engage with hazard maps directly and take part in the decision-making process. In conversations that informed the game’s development, Ravela heard people whose livelihoods are vulnerable to climate events voice immediate concerns about what would happen if a future season failed: “If I don’t plant next season — if I can’t — what would I do?” Ravela wanted to help people think instead about possible choices, different paths, and their respective risks.

When he asked himself what circumstances allow someone to think about risk, the answer began to take shape. “Well, roll a die. Toss a coin,” he thought. “And where do you do these things? In a game.”

How it works

The process the collaborating team developed takes place in three stages. The first is a “snakes and ladders” game, played with physical game pieces and tokens. Once players become comfortable with the mixed game, the final stage, developed by Ravela, abandons the board game and moves fully into a more detailed computer simulation that can be played on a cellphone app.

The three villages lie in a coastal region that faces numerous extreme weather events threatening water availability and agricultural productivity. As riverbeds rise from sediment accumulation over time and the land sinks from groundwater extraction, saltwater can more easily intrude into groundwater aquifers, while freshwater drainage, recharge, and flushing become increasingly difficult, intensifying waterlogging and drought.

“There’s a vicious cycle that’s happening with salinization of the soil,” Ravela explains.

articles.summary: Future focused: An upcoming event will connect broadband service providers with what's emerging and ahead in their industry.
articles.content:
C3 Technology Summit: Where industry insight meets innovation
Aug. 31, 2026
This piece is sponsored by SDN Communications.
The broadband industry has never stood still, but today’s pace of change is unlike anything we’ve experienced before.
Artificial intelligence is transforming network operations. Cybersecurity threats are becoming more sophisticated. Regulatory requirements continue to evolve. Customers expect more bandwidth, more reliability and more content than ever before. At the same time, service providers are challenged to make strategic investments while maintaining resilient, future-ready networks.
That’s exactly why the C3 Technology Summit exists.
The 2025 C3 event held at the Canopy by Hilton.
Hosted by SDN Communications, the annual summit brings together industry experts for two days dedicated to one goal: preparing service providers for the future of connectivity.
Designed around industry priorities
The name C3 represents the three pillars that define the event:
- Connectivity
- Capacity
- Content
Rather than offering broad, high-level discussions, C3 focuses on practical strategies providers can take back to their organizations. This year’s agenda reflects that commitment.
Sessions will explore topics such as:
- Data centers
- DDoS mitigation and cybersecurity
- Telecommunications regulatory updates
- Artificial intelligence
- Unmanned aircraft systems for telecommunications
Together, these sessions create a comprehensive look at both today’s operational priorities and tomorrow’s emerging technologies.
Learning from industry peers
One of the defining characteristics of C3 is its speakers.
Rather than hearing only from keynote personalities or industry commentators, attendees learn directly from professionals who are actively solving the same challenges providers face every day.
Technology leaders from organizations such as Akamai, Corero Network Security, Sunbird Software, Geosolv, NTCA, SDTA, Airborne Defense, Eide Bailly and more will share practical insights, real-world experiences and proven strategies.
Collaboration continued beyond the sessions
One of the greatest strengths of the broadband industry has always been its willingness to collaborate. The C3 Technology Summit creates an environment where conversations continue well beyond the presentation room.
Whether during meals, sponsor showcases or networking receptions, attendees have the opportunity to exchange ideas with peers who understand the unique challenges of operating broadband and middle-mile networks. Many attendees discover that someone else has already solved the problem they’re facing. Those conversations often become just as valuable as the sessions.
Guests and vendors enjoying time together at C3 in 2025.
Middle-mile providers
Many telecommunications conferences understandably focus on consumer services or national carriers.
Middle-mile providers serve critical infrastructure connecting communities, regional providers, enterprises, healthcare organizations, educational institutions, public safety agencies and wireless carriers.
The C3 Technology Summit recognizes this unique role.
Discussions intentionally are relevant to organizations responsible for building, maintaining and expanding the networks that power regional connectivity.
It’s an opportunity to engage with peers facing similar realities while learning from experts who understand the industry’s unique challenges.
Attendees enjoying a session.
The importance of resiliency
Security incidents, severe weather, equipment failures and unexpected network disruptions all require providers to respond quickly while keeping customers connected.
That’s why several sessions at this year’s summit focus on building stronger, more resilient networks. These conversations will explore the strategies that help keep networks running through every unexpected disruption, staying on when communities need them most.
Join the conversation
The 2026 C3 Technology Summit will be Sept. 28–29 at the Canopy by Hilton in downtown Sioux Falls.
With focused educational sessions, meaningful networking opportunities and discussions centered on the future of connectivity, capacity and content, the summit offers attendees new voices and unique perspectives.
In an industry where technology changes rapidly and collaboration is essential, taking time to learn from peers and industry experts is one of the most valuable investments a provider can make.
The future of broadband won’t be built by one organization alone. It will be built by providers willing to come together, share knowledge and innovate together — that’s exactly what the C3 Technology Summit is designed to do.

articles.summary: John Ternus takes over as Apple's chief executive on Tuesday, inheriting a company that towers over the smartphone market but trails its rivals in artificial intelligence.Ives expects the new chief executive to lean into what he knows.
articles.content:
- AAPL -0.89%

John Ternus takes over as Apple's chief executive on Tuesday, inheriting a company that towers over the smartphone market but trails its rivals in artificial intelligence.

One of his biggest challenges will be balancing the company's dependence on China while parrying acute political pressure from the White House.

The handover ends Tim Cook's 15-year run, replacing the operations specialist who built Apple's supply chain with the engineer who built its hardware.

Ternus, 51, joined Apple's design team in 2001 and worked his way up to senior vice president of hardware engineering, reporting to Cook.

He leads the engineering teams behind Apple's entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company's revenue.

He gets barely a week to settle in, with Apple holding its annual iPhone event on September 9, where it is expected to unveil its first foldable handset.

"Tim Cook left the house in phenomenal order," said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at investment firm Yorkville Ives & Co.

"But now it's about Ternus defining the AI chapter."

Ives expects the new chief executive to lean into what he knows.

"There's no reason to fix what's already working," he said, predicting Ternus will concentrate on hardware innovation while leaving Cook's supply chain intact.

Some analysts had argued software chief Craig Federighi was the more logical pick for a company scrambling to catch up on AI.

Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies, said that misreads how consumers actually adopt technology.

"Consumers are still buying hardware first, and it's going to be like that for a long time," she said. "You're not going to discover the value of AI if you're not interested in the hardware."

Cook echoed that sentiment in a final memo to employees on Monday.

"Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does," Cook wrote.

Ternus earned a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and worked as an engineer at Virtual Research Systems before joining Apple.

Inside the company he is credited with driving a push to make products more durable, reliable and resilient, and with design work that cut their carbon footprint.

The harder question is what kind of leader he becomes.

"Even people that know him now don't know him as a CEO," Milanesi said.

"You might know him as the head of engineering, but once you're CEO, things change. Your responsibility is bigger, your power is bigger. You're dancing a different kind of dance."

- 'Learn on the job' -

Nowhere is that gap wider than in the geopolitical role Cook excelled at, courting both Beijing and Donald Trump's White House to protect a supply chain that runs largely through China.

Apple's manufacturing operation is among the most complex in corporate history, a web of hundreds of suppliers and assembly lines that Cook painstakingly built over decades.

Cook in recent years began shifting some of the work elsewhere -- iPhone assembly to India, other production to Vietnam -- but the diversification has been gradual with China, one of Apple's biggest consumer markets, still anchoring the system.

Complicating matters, Trump has repeatedly demanded Apple build iPhones on American soil, threatening tariffs on those made overseas.

Cook avoided the heaviest blows of Trump's trade war by cultivating the president directly, making US investment commitments and political donations -- all while also keeping Beijing onside.

The tricky political terrain will be new for Ternus.

"He knows Apple Park like the back of his pocket in terms of hardware," Ives said of Ternus. "But on the global stage -- that's probably one of the biggest areas where he's going to have to learn on the job."

Cook is not going far. He becomes executive chairman of Apple's board on the same day, with a mandate the company has said includes engaging policymakers around the world.

"That was really clever," said Milanesi, arguing the arrangement frees Ternus from a role Cook has handled alone for years.

The September 9 iPhone event will be the first public measure of the handover.

A foldable iPhone would be the most significant redesign in years, and Ternus will be its face -- eight days into the job.

"This is a moment that they created for him," Milanesi said.

Cook in recent years began shifting some of the work elsewhere -- iPhone assembly to India, other production to Vietnam -- but the diversification has been gradual with China, one of Apple's biggest consumer markets, still anchoring the system.

Complicating matters, Trump has repeatedly demanded Apple build iPhones on American soil, threatening tariffs on those made overseas. 

Cook avoided the heaviest blows of Trump's trade war by cultivating the president directly, making US investment commitments and political donations -- all while also keeping Beijing onside. 

The tricky political terrain will be new for Ternus. 

"He knows Apple Park like the back of his pocket in terms of hardware," Ives said of Ternus. "But on the global stage -- that's probably one of the biggest areas where he's going to have to learn on the job."

Cook is not going far. He becomes executive chairman of Apple's board on the same day, with a mandate the company has said includes engaging policymakers around the world.

"That was really clever," said Milanesi, arguing the arrangement frees Ternus from a role Cook has handled alone for years.

The September 9 iPhone event will be the first public measure of the handover. 

A foldable iPhone would be the most significant redesign in years, and Ternus will be its face -- eight days into the job.

"This is a moment that they created for him," Milanesi said.

articles.heading: Facial recognition technology 'scope creep' is upon us, experts warn
articles.summary: Industry groups say the move to facial scans in supermarkets is about safety, but analysts say that once the technology is installed, its "scope creep" paves the way for options like discriminatory pricing.
articles.content:
Facial recognition technology 'scope creep' is upon us, experts warn
A shopper walks into a supermarket and grabs a basket. By that time, a camera has scanned their face.
That is what experts warn could be the new normal for Australians.
Supermarkets started with exit gates and bagging-area cameras. Now they are trialling facial recognition technology.
In August, Coles and Woolworths rolled out facial recognition technology trials in a bid to combat crime with about a third of retail workers not feeling safe in their workplace, according to a union survey of about 3,000 staff.
The technology scans the features of a person's face to create a unique digital code and identify them.
Neither of the supermarket giants has said if it would be rolled out in their Australian stores.
However, both companies said they were looking into improving protection for their customers and staff.
Industry groups say the move is about safety, but experts warn once the technology is installed the "scope creep" does not stop.
'Scope creep'
Scope creep, also known as function creep, is when society incrementally allows things to happen over time that people feel uncomfortable about.
"We let it pass and all of a sudden you see a layering of the technology being used for more privacy-intrusive purposes," said responsible technology policy specialist Lauren Perry from the University of Technology Sydney.
She is concerned face scans could shift from safety and security to customer experience in ways that could disadvantage and harm the consumer.
The layering of new technologies such as face scan-enabled EFTPOS machines and the widespread rollout of digital price tags across supermarkets could tailor the real-life shopping experience.
"I hear people say, 'I don't really care about my personal information that much. It's all over the internet anyway. I've got nothing to hide,'" she said.
"You've only got one face. You can change your password if it gets hacked … but you can't change your face.
"Would every single person who walks into a supermarket have to give up their sensitive biometric data to buy a bottle of milk?"
Facial data gives companies more information about consumer purchasing behaviour and how they move through the store, paving the way for options like discriminatory pricing, Ms Perry said.
"Now they have your face, they have your loyalty card, your bank card, they can piece together a pretty clear picture of individual shopping behaviours," she said.
"For example, supermarkets know that a lot of women visit suburban grocery stores with their kids at the end of the school day. They could use this information to jack up the prices of things like lunch box foods at those stores."
A Coles spokesperson told the ABC: "While no decision has been made about the use of this technology, we absolutely reject any claim that this technology would be used to monitor team or regular shoppers, or for marketing or pricing purposes."
Surveillance tech can alter our behaviour
Kiley Seymour, a neuroscience and behaviour researcher, said adopting face scans in supermarkets was another form of surveillance that changed how people behave.
She said being watched could unconsciously alter mental processes that made us more hypervigilant and tuned into threats around us.
"We might experience more social anxiety and paranoia in our society as surveillance increases," she said.
"This puts our brains into this threat detection and fight mode without us even realising it.
"If our brains are always in this hypervigilant state due to surveillance, that could have other impacts that are similar to psychosis. For instance, leading to paranoid thoughts and beliefs."
'Locked out of the supermarket'
Experts warn that face scans do not work the same for everyone.
Surveillance expert Mark Andrejevic from Monash University said the technology was historically less accurate for people with darker skin, women and older people, leading to more mix-ups.
"We have seen instances in the United Kingdom of people being wrongly banned from shops because of an incorrect match," he said.
UK shoppers told The Guardian they were unable to challenge the companies after being falsely identified.
Mr Andrejevic was particularly concerned with systems that had no option for customers to challenge the outcomes.
"Are you banned for life from all supermarkets if you walk out with a pack of chewing gum?" he said.
Australia has no facial recognition law
Facial recognition technology is one of the biggest privacy risks Australians face today, with almost 90 per cent of the population more concerned about it than they were five years ago, according to a government survey this year.
Australia does not have a dedicated facial recognition law.
Instead, it is governed by the Privacy Act, which does not explicitly ban or permit its use.
Mr Andrejevic said retail outlets had not been transparent about their use of the technology.
"If they want to put us all in databases there needs to be some very clear guidelines and regulations about how this works," he said.
"Accuracy and bias ratings for the technology being used should be publicly available and a notification should be provided to people who are included in the database."

articles.article_title: ‘Backwards and poor’: Trump issues dire warning to communities blocking critical technology
articles.heading: ‘Backwards and poor’: Trump issues dire warning to communities blocking critical technology
articles.summary: President Donald Trump warned communities rejecting data centers risk becoming "backwards and poor" as states battle over AI boom energy and water costs.
articles.content:
Americans have relied on data centers for decades — most don’t realize how much of their lives run through them

AI executive Brittany Kaiser explains how every time you scroll, stream or search, a data center is working behind the scenes to power your digital life.

President Donald Trump took aim Monday at the growing backlash against data centers, warning that communities that shut the door on the facilities risk missing out on the jobs and economic gains of America's AI boom.

"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," he added.

Trump has made energy dominance and U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence central pillars of his second term, placing data centers at the center of his push to maintain America's edge over China.

"China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement," Trump wrote, arguing that resistance to new facilities risks undercutting America's edge in the global AI race.

ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI

President Donald Trump has made energy dominance and artificial intelligence key priorities for his second term. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The data center boom has also emerged as a midterm flashpoint, as concerns over rising electricity costs , water use and rapid development collide with promises of jobs, investment and U.S. dominance in artificial intelligence.

That tension is already playing out across the country.

Trump has specifically criticized Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's approach , calling the Lone Star State's stance toward data centers a "mistake" and pointing to the economic investment the projects can bring to communities willing to host them.

Texas has cemented its status as a heavyweight in the industry, with Dallas ranking as the world's No. 1 primary data center market in Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 Global Data Center Market Comparison. But billions of dollars in new investment have also brought enormous electricity demands and questions over who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support the boom.

Abbott has moved to address those concerns, directing regulators to ensure data centers cover the infrastructure costs needed to serve them and calling on developers to add their own power generation rather than shift costs onto Texas residents.

A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD'S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

Texas leaders, including Gov. Greg Abbott, have sought to position the state as a destination for large-scale data center development even as officials grapple with the strain new projects could place on the electric grid. (Antranik Tavitian/Reuters)

Meanwhile, in Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro recently imposed new requirements on large data center developments.

Other governors have taken a more restrictive stance. Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyper-scale data centers as states grapple with concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and the pace of development.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Data center development is surging across the Lone Star State, with North Texas taking the top spot in a new global ranking of the industry’s leading markets. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/Contributor/AFP/Getty Images)

Data centers house the servers and computing equipment that power artificial intelligence and cloud services, requiring vast amounts of electricity to operate and cool. Most Americans may never see the inside of one, but they rely on data centers constantly, often without realizing it .

The growing patchwork of state restrictions and requirements could complicate Trump’s push for rapid data center expansion as communities weigh America’s AI ambitions against concerns over electricity costs, water use and development.
