articles.article_title: Hugging Face hack could indicate cultural issues at OpenAI
articles.heading: Hugging Face hack could indicate cultural issues at OpenAI
articles.summary: Alarm bells within the company should have stopped model training from going forward. So why didn’t they?
articles.content:
Hugging Face hack could indicate cultural issues at OpenAI
Alarm bells within the company should have stopped model training from going forward. So why didn’t they?
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
By now you’ve probably heard about last month’s major AI security incident, in which OpenAI agents escaped their sandbox and hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face while trying to cheat on a test. It’s a wild story. On Wednesday, OpenAI released a postmortem technical report on the incident, which I wrote about here.
The day before OpenAI released that report, I spoke with David Krueger, a computer science professor and prominent alignment expert who took leave from the University of Montreal to found and lead an AI safety nonprofit called Evitable. He said what he had really hoped to see in the report was an analysis of the human factors behind the incident.
“When you look at accidents and incidents, oftentimes people try to find the technical source of failure, but that can give a very inaccurate and misleading sense of why the failure occurred,” he said. “If people are just cutting corners all the time, if people are not in a culture that prioritizes safety and has appropriate incentives and structures, [accidents] are kind of bound to happen.”
The report did not meet Krueger’s hopes. Its 38 pages detail a multi-month progression of agent misbehavior that culminated in the Hugging Face hack, explore the technical reasons why that misbehavior occurred, and enumerate the steps being taken to prevent similar events in the future. But there’s no consideration of the role that company culture may have played in the incident, and the report includes few references to specific human errors.
That’s all the more concerning because the references to human error in the report suggest that significant cultural issues could be at play. Back in May, models in training figured out how to communicate with one another via an improvised message board, and an OpenAI team observed the behavior. Because that behavior occurred during training, the models learned that secret interagent communication was a viable strategy for completing tasks—but rather than restarting the training process, the team allowed the models to move forward with that risky information encoded in their weights.
When those models were tested in late June, they again created a message board, which enabled the Hugging Face attack. This message board, too, was discovered, but the employees who responded determined that evaluation could continue, and the report suggests that no one higher up the chain of command realized what was going on until it was far too late.
“For this to have gotten this out of control in this way requires a very long series of failures, a cascading set of failures that cause an increasingly large footprint that if at any point a human notices and raises the alarm, this should end,” says Zvi Mowshowitz, a popular AI safety writer on Substack who has drawn attention to OpenAI’s failure to halt training after the first message board was discovered. According to the report, OpenAI employees noticed what was happening at multiple points—and either failed to raise the alarm or were not heard when they did.
What OpenAI’s report fails to address is why a company that develops such high-risk systems did not prevent this severe communication breakdown, though Mowshowitz has his suspicions. “All these different failures are all pointing in the same direction, which is that the safety culture at OpenAI doesn’t exist or is anemically weak,” he says.
Of course, just because we don’t see a deep analysis of safety factors in the report doesn’t mean that OpenAI isn’t conducting one internally. But in an email to MIT Technology Review, Johns Hopkins University professor emeritus and organizational safety expert Kathleen Sutcliffe expressed concern that the public report did not include any reflection on the company’s practices and culture. “The ways in which people interact—the daily habits, routines, and practices we engage in in our organizational lives—affect our abilities to be alert and aware of unfolding events, our abilities to make sense of what we see, and ultimately our abilities to cope with events as they unfold,” she wrote.
In response to questions about whether and how the company is reflecting on its safety culture, OpenAI referred MIT Technology Review back to the technical report.
We do know that at least some high-level reflection on safety procedures has taken place at OpenAI, because the technical report does make clear that the company is updating its protocols for responding to safety incidents. But culture change is a tricky problem, and without more information from the company, it’s difficult to say whether strengthened response protocols alone will do much to prevent a future crisis.
In its report, OpenAI spends a great deal of time reflecting on the failures in alignment between the AI models the company trains and tests and the humans who run them. But even bigger alignment problems may exist in the disconnect between company culture and the public interest. And as tough as technical AI research might be, fixing those problems could prove far harder.

articles.summary: The governor of the Bank of England warned of AI's “volatility” caused by energy shocks from the US-Iran war.
articles.content:
AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20
The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.
Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.
In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".
Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.
Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

articles.article_title: How Seattle Public Schools Is Rethinking Technology
articles.heading: Seattle Met
articles.summary: A new superintendent banned phones at Seattle Public Schools, but some parents want to go even further.
articles.content:
Parents Are Rethinking School Tech
On Wednesday, September 2, bells will ring for more than 40,000 students to signal the first day of school at Seattle Public Schools (unless a teacher strike intervenes). But phones will not.
Last spring, superintendent Ben Shuldiner announced no-phone policies for grades K-12; they went into effect May 4, his 100th day in office. Before his hiring he’d promised to address various issues—closing the budget deficit, increasing student enrollment, ensuring student safety in schools—but this addressed a hot (power) button topic: screen time in the classroom.
Since the early days of Saturday morning cartoons, popular and scientific belief has held that screens can have a negative effect on childhood development. Half a decade after remote learning went into hyperdrive during the pandemic, making Zoom classrooms and online coursework a daily reality, parents and educators are trying to find balance.
SPS is hardly ahead of the pack on phones. Twenty-two states already prohibit them in schools outright, and in June, Governor Bob Ferguson introduced a proposal for a statewide ban. He did it at Robert Eagle Staff Middle School in Northgate, which implemented its own ban in 2024.
“Ninety percent of my job, and my counselors’ job, was just playing whack-a-mole and putting out fires from having the tech in the building,” principal Zachary Stowell says. While phones are nominally a way to communicate, he and his team found that they instead silo students.
Two years into the ban, Stowell has already seen the benefits. “We went from fights at lunch in the bathroom...to dancing and connecting, and having a good time at lunch.”
But it’s only one part of a larger conversation surrounding technology use in schools. Parents are questioning not only the tiny distraction machines kids bring from home, but also the ones handed out by teachers.
“We’re a very screen-light family; we’ve just always avoided screens,” says Hilary Patterson, a former Seattle Public Schools teacher and current SPS parent. She was surprised when her kindergartner came home from school with an iPad—standard through second grade in the district. Third through twelfth graders receive laptops. “We don’t have iPads [at home], because we just don’t want to have to deal with regulating it.”
The district’s lofty goal is to create equity among students regardless of their ability to afford their own devices. However, parents like Patterson are concerned about how they’re being used in the classroom. Last November, she attended a PTA meeting at James Baldwin Elementary featuring Emily Cherkin, a Seattle activist who founded what she calls the Tech-Intentional Movement.
“We need Tech Ed, not Ed Tech,” Cherkin says, making a distinction between what she describes as a for-profit industry—Ed Tech—and the more beneficial technical education, “a way of teaching children about things they need to know.” She claims that once curriculums are built around the technology and state testing is administered online, teachers find themselves leaning on screens as their time and resources are limited.
EdTech includes devices like laptops and iPads but also games like Quizlet and Kahoot! and platforms like YouTube or Google Workspace; teacher-led lessons can include them all. Cherkin questions whether they could have negative effects on students, pointing to a landmark Los Angeles case that found Meta and YouTube liable for creating addictive platforms for children.
“In their discovery materials, YouTube admits that their viewership was down during school hours and they say, ‘Well, how do we get kids back on YouTube during the school day?’ And their solution was by pitching it as an educational tool,” Cherkin says.
After hearing Cherkin speak, Patterson teamed up with fellow parent Erica Shutes-
David to create Seattle Families for Intentional Tech. More than 800 parents signed a petition that the group shared with the district in April asking for a number of things, including parental consent for data-collecting products, screentime limits by grade, and allowing and supporting teachers and students to use paper-based alternatives.
Katie Davis is a co-founder and co-director of the Center for Digital Youth at the University of Washington; she says that her research finds that limiting the negative effects of technology isn’t as simple as reducing the use of those tools. “[Tech] doesn’t usually transform, but maybe it makes something a little bit easier to do,” Davis says. “If you look at the literature, there’s a lot of examples of technologies that don’t have any effect at all on student outcomes.”
Principal Stowell of Robert Eagle Staff Middle School says money is part of the issue. “School funding comes in different buckets, and sometimes there’s not funding here, but there’s funding in tech,” Stowell says. “I think sometimes technology is a little more cost-effective than consumables, but the reality is, what’s best for our kids?” Still, he looked for ways to rein in technology use in the classroom. He hopes to reintroduce laptop carts, meaning students wouldn’t have access to the devices at all times.
“We’re starting to craft and plant seeds around what does it look like to minimize, even at lunch, some of the technology use as a whole?” Stowell says. “We were pioneers in the cell phone thing, why don’t we be pioneers in reinventing what it is to check laptops back out?”
The principal says a clearer direction needs to come from the top down, preferably statewide. As it stands, the SPS directive from May only addresses a single screen—phones. “When it’s not clear, then everyone’s doing [a] rogue thing…we can unintentionally penalize those that are already historically marginalized,” he says. “When policy is clear, then we can implement with fidelity, with joy, with humanity.” And without the dings, rings, or a glowing screen.

articles.title: Pipeline of Talent: ConocoPhillips Alaska Process Technology Support Fund

articles.article_title: Pipeline of Talent: ConocoPhillips Alaska Process Technology Support Fund - Alaska Business Magazine
articles.heading: Pipeline of Talent: ConocoPhillips Alaska Process Technology Support Fund
articles.summary: The ConocoPhillips Alaska Process Technology Support Fund helps prepare students to operate and maintain complex industrial systems.
articles.content:
Pipeline of Talent: ConocoPhillips Alaska Process Technology Support Fund
To help meet Alaska’s growing workforce needs, companies are forming innovative partnerships with educators around the state. One example is ConocoPhillips Alaska, which recently donated $400,000 to the University of Alaska (UA) to establish the Process Technology Support Fund. The fund supports process technology programs in Fairbanks at UAF Community and Technical College (CTC) and at UAA’s Kenai Peninsula College (KPC), helping pay for equipment and technology upgrades as well as expanded outreach.
“This is the right time because the workforce need is real and immediate and because UA’s process technology programs already deliver strong outcomes,” says Tim Turner, vice president of operations at ConocoPhillips Alaska. “We see this as a long-term workforce development investment that connects classroom learning to real careers, and we hope it also encourages additional industry partners to invest in this vital pipeline.”
The UA System has long had a strong relationship with ConocoPhillips—its largest corporate donor—which has invested nearly $45 million over four decades. That support has reinforced the value of private-sector investment in workforce training. UAF CTC Dean Kevin Alexander says ConocoPhillips’ latest donation may be the largest single cash gift he has seen directed to any UAF CTC program. In his view, the contribution reflects both the urgency of Alaska’s workforce needs and the strength of the partnership behind the effort.
Awareness and Access
Process technology refers to the equipment and methods for controlling industrial systems, such as oil and gas pipelines, refineries, or heavy machinery in power plants and factories. According to Turner, ConocoPhillips and its peers depend on highly skilled process technicians and operators to keep critical infrastructure running safely and reliably. With twenty years at ConocoPhillips in engineering and production operations leadership roles in the Lower 48 and the Alaska Business Unit, he has seen firsthand how essential these professionals are to safe day-to-day operations and long-term workforce sustainability.
“The need is growing, and the challenge is twofold: awareness and access,” he says. “Too few Alaskans—especially students in rural communities—know this career path exists, and training programs need the modern tools and reach to prepare students for today’s operating environments. This initiative helps close those gaps by expanding early exposure for high school students, modernizing hands-on training, and creating clearer pathways from classroom to good-paying, in-demand careers in Alaska.”
David Fonger, UAF CTC’s process technology program coordinator, also sees strong demand for both process technicians and instrumentation technicians across Alaska, especially in the oil and gas industry. “Many operators in the field are close to retirement age,” says Fonger, who also serves as a process technology assistant professor and advisor at UAF. “The Alaska LNG [liquefied natural gas] project is going to create an even larger demand for operators in the future.”
A Great Place to Start
The ConocoPhillips Alaska Process Technology Support Fund is designed to strengthen programs where students learn—in labs, classrooms, and communities—while also expanding flexible access. In Fairbanks, for example, the fund will help modernize hands-on training with updated instructional equipment and simulation technology so students can practice on tools that mirror real operating environments. “Statewide, UA’s high school bridging approach makes it possible for students to earn college credit early through a three-credit introductory process technology course that can be offered both in-person and online,” Turner says.
On the Kenai Peninsula, the fund supports outreach through the “Taste of College” program and a train-the-teachers model—enabled by portable simulation equipment—so more high schools can offer dual-credit process technology courses. Support is also available to help students take the next step after high school. Turner explains, “We’ve also launched a scholarship fund at the Alaska Community Foundation for those students pursuing the two-year process technology degree through the University of Alaska—whether they attend in Fairbanks or on the Kenai Peninsula.”
For ConocoPhillips, Turner says, workforce development is not abstract; it is reflected every day in the people who keep operations safe and running. “Many ConocoPhillips Alaska operators started in the University of Alaska process technology programs, and we know the value of graduates arriving with strong fundamentals and hands-on experience,” he explains. “Our involvement helps ensure the training stays aligned with real-world needs: emphasizing safety culture, reliability, problem-solving, and the technologies students will see on the job.”
“Too few Alaskans—especially students in rural communities—know this career path exists, and training programs need the modern tools and reach to prepare students for today’s operating environments. This initiative helps close those gaps.”
Jesse Thomas, a facility supervisor at Kuparuk River Unit and UAF Process Technology graduate.
Tim Turner, vice president of operations for ConocoPhillips Alaska, oversees North Slope operations, including production, maintenance, and operational excellence initiatives.
Realistic, Hands-on Training
“Our message to students is: if you’re looking for a hands-on, high-responsibility career with strong long-term demand, process technology is a great place to start,” Turner says.
UAF CTC’s process technology program prepares students for careers in oil and gas production, mining and milling, transportation and refining, chemical manufacturing, power generation, utilities, wastewater treatment, and food processing. The students work with the same kinds of systems, controls, valves, pumps, and industrial safety expectations they will encounter on the job. The program is aligned with the North American Process Technology Alliance, meaning the curriculum matches national industry standards.
Fonger describes UAF CTC’s process technology program as a comprehensive two-year associate of science degree that focuses on several key areas: safety, knowledge, hands-on learning, and experience. The program leases an off-campus, 6,500-square-foot facility with classroom space and a hands-on shop, creating an in-person learning environment with remote access capability. “This allows each student to gain an understanding of the lecture topic and then complete various hands-on activities to allow a better understanding and knowledge of the topic,” Fonger says.
The program’s shop includes hands-on trainers as well as an operational plant with a control room. The plant is used in a variety of classes, from introduction to process technology to piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID), operations, systems, and troubleshooting. Students prepare for real-world work environments through a safety minute before class, job safety analysis before any hands-on activity, and safety briefings, along with personal protective equipment for each situation.
Students also write plant start-up and operating procedures, which are tested and revised as needed. They use simulators to experience what it’s like to sit in the operator’s seat—starting up equipment, running operations, troubleshooting problems, and handling issues that happen during the simulation. “Parameters are input by the instructor beforehand to simulate a variety of possible issues,” Fonger explains. “This is to see how the student deals with these different scenarios.”
There are no educational prerequisites for entry into the process technology program at UAF CTC, which also offers on-demand tours of the facility. “If you are in high school, reach out and we can talk about the program, classes, and a timeline to complete the degree,” Fonger says. “Adults who are interested in the program, have questions, or are ready to sign up, can also reach out to me.”
Path Full of Opportunities
During the spring 2026 semester, eighty students were enrolled in UAF CTC’s process technology program, including full-time, part-time, in-person, and remote or distance learners. “We have quite a few students who currently work on the North Slope of Alaska or other process technology fields that are also enrolled and actively taking classes either in person or remotely,” he says.
That’s Richard Goss’ situation as a student at KPC. Goss already works on the Slope as an equipment engineer, and he completes most of his coursework online. He describes KPC’s process technology program as “excellent” and professors as “wildly accommodating” with scheduling. “P&ID drawing assignments—where we walk down Big Silver (the training process system on campus) and draw out flow paths—have been excellent,” he says. “I’m a hands-on learner, so the exercise really helps solidify the relationships between vessels, their control elements, and their measurement elements. Our Simtronics work, where we use a simulator to ‘control’ a process like a furnace, is also great for illustrating the cause-and-effect relationships between inputs and controllable variables.”
Through the program, Goss expects to gain the skills he needs to learn effectively and absorb knowledge from more experienced professionals. That foundation, he says, will help him become a capable operator who can support the growth and success of those around him.
“There isn’t a scenario where enrollment doesn’t help you in some way. You could enroll, love the program, and set off on a path full of incredible opportunities with some of the major players in the industry,” he says.
KPC’s process technology program has a strong track record. According to recent institutional data, 88 percent of KPC process technology graduates land jobs in their field within one year of graduation. Average first-year earnings exceed $84,000, and the average wage rises to about $130,000 within five years.
Expanding Capacity for Growing Demand
Whereas a process technology education trains operators to monitor entire industrial systems, an instrumentation certification deals with the installation, calibration, and repair of the sensors and valves that enable the control of those systems. UAF also offers an instrumentation certification program that complements the process technology program. The Certificate in Instrumentation Technology gives students entry-level skills in industrial instrumentation through state-of-the-art equipment and hands-on training. It also prepares them to take the entry-level International Society of Automation (ISA) certificate exam, a nationally recognized credential.
Fonger says many students study process technology and instrumentation at the same time. Doing so typically means taking three or four additional classes, depending on course load, but students finish with both a process technology degree and an instrumentation certification. That combination can make them more competitive job applicants. “ConocoPhillips has expressed interest in the instrumentation program expanding to include automation and other high-tech components,” Fonger says. “We have answered the request by adding three classes to help prepare for the automation as well as revamping another class to include automation.”
The UAF Process Technology lab, located at the Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center, offers flexible course schedules and virtual lectures, making the program more accessible for adults balancing jobs and families.
While UA is making strides in strengthening its curriculum, it’s also facing several challenges. One is how to increase enrollment. UA wants to preserve a strong hands-on component while serving as many students as possible, Alexander says. That is a constant balancing act because process technology training requires specialized equipment and dedicated space.
Programs with an online component reach more students, while hands-on portions are scheduled as space allows. For now, that is the most effective way to manage growing enrollment. At the same time, the university is looking strategically at how to expand its physical footprint—even as rising costs make that more difficult—so it can accommodate more students and meet workforce demand.
“Every trade sector is showing an increase,” Alexander says. “And, if we’re being honest, the state of Alaska is a little bit behind the power curve in building capacity to meet that demand. But that speaks to state budget challenges and massively increasing costs that are out of everyone’s control. It’s nobody’s fault really, but that’s where we are… Investments like the ConocoPhillips Process Technology Support Fund help maximize enrollments at least to our capacity as we look at ways to build.”
Sustained Commitment
Alexander says he hopes UA’s strong relationship with ConocoPhillips will continue. Ongoing industry support could help address one of the university’s top priorities: faculty recruitment. Alaska’s demand for skilled workers has pushed private-sector wages to unprecedented levels, which benefits workers but makes recruiting and retaining faculty in trade programs increasingly difficult.
“My hope is that there’s a future where there is faculty salary support or the idea of a sponsored faculty where a large company like Conoco is simply paying a salary that’s competitive with the private sector so that we can recruit folks,” Alexander says. “Or there’s a partnership where they take a competent, qualified instrumentation technician and pay them to come teach for us on a temporary basis and we rotate their expertise through the classroom.”
Long term, Turner says ConocoPhillips would like its partnership with UA to make process technology a well-known, accessible path to stable, high-demand careers—especially for Alaska students who might not otherwise know about or see themselves in these roles. For Turner, success means more students earning early college credit, more modern training capacity, and more graduates stepping into jobs across Alaska’s critical industries.
“On our side, we’re also expanding career on-ramps—our goal is to increase our process tech/operator summer interns each year and offer a stronger pipeline of operator apprenticeships for post-graduates,” he says. “Together, those pieces help sustain a workforce that can support safe operations and long-term economic vitality for Alaska.”

For ConocoPhillips, Turner says, workforce development is not abstract; it is reflected every day in the people who keep operations safe and running. “Many ConocoPhillips Alaska operators started in the University of Alaska process technology programs, and we know the value of graduates arriving with strong fundamentals and hands-on experience,” he explains. “Our involvement helps ensure the training stays aligned with real-world needs: emphasizing safety culture, reliability, problem-solving, and the technologies students will see on the job.”

“Too few Alaskans—especially students in rural communities—know this career path exists, and training programs need the modern tools and reach to prepare students for today’s operating environments. This initiative helps close those gaps.”

—Tim Turner, Vice President of Operations, ConocoPhillips Alaska

Jesse Thomas, a facility supervisor at Kuparuk River Unit and UAF Process Technology graduate.

Photo Credit: ConocoPhillips Alaska

Tim Turner, vice president of operations for ConocoPhillips Alaska, oversees North Slope operations, including production, maintenance, and operational excellence initiatives.

Photo Credit: ConocoPhillips Alaska

Realistic, Hands-on Training

“Our message to students is: if you’re looking for a hands-on, high-responsibility career with strong long-term demand, process technology is a great place to start,” Turner says.

UAF CTC’s process technology program prepares students for careers in oil and gas production, mining and milling, transportation and refining, chemical manufacturing, power generation, utilities, wastewater treatment, and food processing. The students work with the same kinds of systems, controls, valves, pumps, and industrial safety expectations they will encounter on the job. The program is aligned with the North American Process Technology Alliance, meaning the curriculum matches national industry standards.

Fonger describes UAF CTC’s process technology program as a comprehensive two-year associate of science degree that focuses on several key areas: safety, knowledge, hands-on learning, and experience. The program leases an off-campus, 6,500-square-foot facility with classroom space and a hands-on shop, creating an in-person learning environment with remote access capability. “This allows each student to gain an understanding of the lecture topic and then complete various hands-on activities to allow a better understanding and knowledge of the topic,” Fonger says.

The program’s shop includes hands-on trainers as well as an operational plant with a control room. The plant is used in a variety of classes, from introduction to process technology to piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID), operations, systems, and troubleshooting. Students prepare for real-world work environments through a safety minute before class, job safety analysis before any hands-on activity, and safety briefings, along with personal protective equipment for each situation.

Students also write plant start-up and operating procedures, which are tested and revised as needed. They use simulators to experience what it’s like to sit in the operator’s seat—starting up equipment, running operations, troubleshooting problems, and handling issues that happen during the simulation. “Parameters are input by the instructor beforehand to simulate a variety of possible issues,” Fonger explains. “This is to see how the student deals with these different scenarios.”

There are no educational prerequisites for entry into the process technology program at UAF CTC, which also offers on-demand tours of the facility. “If you are in high school, reach out and we can talk about the program, classes, and a timeline to complete the degree,” Fonger says. “Adults who are interested in the program, have questions, or are ready to sign up, can also reach out to me.”

Path Full of Opportunities

During the spring 2026 semester, eighty students were enrolled in UAF CTC’s process technology program, including full-time, part-time, in-person, and remote or distance learners. “We have quite a few students who currently work on the North Slope of Alaska or other process technology fields that are also enrolled and actively taking classes either in person or remotely,” he says.

That’s Richard Goss’ situation as a student at KPC. Goss already works on the Slope as an equipment engineer, and he completes most of his coursework online. He describes KPC’s process technology program as “excellent” and professors as “wildly accommodating” with scheduling. “P&ID drawing assignments—where we walk down Big Silver (the training process system on campus) and draw out flow paths—have been excellent,” he says. “I’m a hands-on learner, so the exercise really helps solidify the relationships between vessels, their control elements, and their measurement elements. Our Simtronics work, where we use a simulator to ‘control’ a process like a furnace, is also great for illustrating the cause-and-effect relationships between inputs and controllable variables.”

Through the program, Goss expects to gain the skills he needs to learn effectively and absorb knowledge from more experienced professionals. That foundation, he says, will help him become a capable operator who can support the growth and success of those around him.

“There isn’t a scenario where enrollment doesn’t help you in some way. You could enroll, love the program, and set off on a path full of incredible opportunities with some of the major players in the industry,” he says.

KPC’s process technology program has a strong track record. According to recent institutional data, 88 percent of KPC process technology graduates land jobs in their field within one year of graduation. Average first-year earnings exceed $84,000, and the average wage rises to about $130,000 within five years.

Expanding Capacity for Growing Demand

Whereas a process technology education trains operators to monitor entire industrial systems, an instrumentation certification deals with the installation, calibration, and repair of the sensors and valves that enable the control of those systems. UAF also offers an instrumentation certification program that complements the process technology program. The Certificate in Instrumentation Technology gives students entry-level skills in industrial instrumentation through state-of-the-art equipment and hands-on training. It also prepares them to take the entry-level International Society of Automation (ISA) certificate exam, a nationally recognized credential.

Fonger says many students study process technology and instrumentation at the same time. Doing so typically means taking three or four additional classes, depending on course load, but students finish with both a process technology degree and an instrumentation certification. That combination can make them more competitive job applicants. “ConocoPhillips has expressed interest in the instrumentation program expanding to include automation and other high-tech components,” Fonger says. “We have answered the request by adding three classes to help prepare for the automation as well as revamping another class to include automation.”

The UAF Process Technology lab, located at the Fairbanks Pipeline Training Center, offers flexible course schedules and virtual lectures, making the program more accessible for adults balancing jobs and families.

Photo Credit: UAF

While UA is making strides in strengthening its curriculum, it’s also facing several challenges. One is how to increase enrollment. UA wants to preserve a strong hands-on component while serving as many students as possible, Alexander says. That is a constant balancing act because process technology training requires specialized equipment and dedicated space.

Programs with an online component reach more students, while hands-on portions are scheduled as space allows. For now, that is the most effective way to manage growing enrollment. At the same time, the university is looking strategically at how to expand its physical footprint—even as rising costs make that more difficult—so it can accommodate more students and meet workforce demand.

“Every trade sector is showing an increase,” Alexander says. “And, if we’re being honest, the state of Alaska is a little bit behind the power curve in building capacity to meet that demand. But that speaks to state budget challenges and massively increasing costs that are out of everyone’s control. It’s nobody’s fault really, but that’s where we are… Investments like the ConocoPhillips Process Technology Support Fund help maximize enrollments at least to our capacity as we look at ways to build.”

Sustained Commitment

Alexander says he hopes UA’s strong relationship with ConocoPhillips will continue. Ongoing industry support could help address one of the university’s top priorities: faculty recruitment. Alaska’s demand for skilled workers has pushed private-sector wages to unprecedented levels, which benefits workers but makes recruiting and retaining faculty in trade programs increasingly difficult.

“My hope is that there’s a future where there is faculty salary support or the idea of a sponsored faculty where a large company like Conoco is simply paying a salary that’s competitive with the private sector so that we can recruit folks,” Alexander says. “Or there’s a partnership where they take a competent, qualified instrumentation technician and pay them to come teach for us on a temporary basis and we rotate their expertise through the classroom.”

Long term, Turner says ConocoPhillips would like its partnership with UA to make process technology a well-known, accessible path to stable, high-demand careers—especially for Alaska students who might not otherwise know about or see themselves in these roles. For Turner, success means more students earning early college credit, more modern training capacity, and more graduates stepping into jobs across Alaska’s critical industries.

“On our side, we’re also expanding career on-ramps—our goal is to increase our process tech/operator summer interns each year and offer a stronger pipeline of operator apprenticeships for post-graduates,” he says. “Together, those pieces help sustain a workforce that can support safe operations and long-term economic vitality for Alaska.”

articles.article_title: Putnam County Sheriff pulls plug on license plate readers amid privacy debate
articles.heading: Putnam County Sheriff pulls plug on license plate readers amid privacy debate
articles.summary: Putnam County Sheriff H.D. “Gator” DeLoach has ordered the immediate disconnection of all automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras in the county, citing growing concerns over privacy, data sharing and the pace of regulation surrounding the technology.
articles.content:
PUTNAM COUNTY, Fla. – Putnam County Sheriff H.D. “Gator” DeLoach has ordered the immediate disconnection of all automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras in the county, citing growing concerns over privacy, data sharing and the pace of regulation surrounding the technology.
DeLoach directed that all 18 cameras — positioned on major roadways throughout Putnam County — be disconnected immediately and fully removed within 30 days.
Recommended Videos
“Over the past several weeks, legitimate questions have continued to emerge regarding privacy, data sharing, governmental oversight and the future regulation of this technology,” DeLoach said. “I believe the responsible course is to discontinue our program and cancel our contract at this time.”
Decision rooted in regulation gap, not technology failure
The move comes amid a broader statewide and national conversation about the appropriate limits of government use of license plate recognition technology.
“This was not a decision I made lightly. ALPR technology has proven to be a valuable law-enforcement tool, but I have become increasingly concerned that the technology is advancing faster than the laws and regulations governing its use. Until that framework catches up and provides clearer, more consistent safeguards for both public safety and individual privacy, I believe discontinuing the program is the most responsible course for our agency and the community we serve,” DeLoach said.
Program helped solve serious crimes since 2022
ALPRs were first deployed in Putnam County in 2022. Since then, the technology aided in locating people with Alzheimer’s disease and early-stage dementia who became disoriented while driving, tracking and arresting murder suspects and — earlier this year — helping the sheriff’s office and the FBI locate a teenage human trafficking victim from another state.
“Automated license plate readers are an effective law-enforcement tool, and I’ve seen firsthand how they can help us locate dangerous offenders, recover stolen vehicles, kidnapping victims and solve serious crimes. I also believe, however, that effective law enforcement requires the trust and confidence of the people we serve,” DeLoach said.
Strong internal safeguards were in place
The sheriff’s office maintained extensive protocols governing ALPR use, including requiring a case number for each instance of access and conducting quarterly audits of the data being accessed. DeLoach emphasized the decision is not a criticism of how his deputies used the technology.
“I remain confident that our deputies used this technology lawfully, responsibly and in accordance with some of the strongest safeguards we could put in place. This decision is not an indictment of their work, nor does it mean the technology has no legitimate law-enforcement value. It simply means that when the rules, public expectations and regulatory environment surrounding a technology are changing this rapidly, we should be willing to reevaluate whether continuing to use it is in the best interest of our community,” DeLoach said.
DeLoach pointed to misuse of ALPR cameras by other law enforcement agencies and private residents across the country as a contributing factor in the decision. The program will remain discontinued until the state legislature establishes clear parameters and guidance for law enforcement use of the technology.
“Public safety matters. So does individual liberty. Neither should be treated casually,” DeLoach said.

articles.title: Triple Tiger Katie Britton cuts winding path through education to lead new technology center
articles.description: Triple Tiger Katie Britton cuts winding path through education to lead new technology center Clemson News
articles.description_html: Triple Tiger Katie Britton cuts winding path through education to lead new technology center  Clemson News
articles.article_title: Triple Tiger Katie Britton cuts winding path through education to lead new technology center
articles.heading: Triple Tiger Katie Britton cuts winding path through education to lead new technology center
articles.summary: Katie Britton uses multiple degrees from Clemson University to positively impact students, families and communities across the School District of Pickens County.
articles.content:
When a Clemson alumnus has 10 characters after their name in the way Katie Britton ’14, M’18, EdD’25 does, it’s safe to say she’s a lifelong fan of the University. However, earning several degrees doesn’t earn someone a spot among the Roaring 10; that happens when degrees turn into impact, and throughout an already varied career, Britton has positively impacted students, families and communities across the School District of Pickens County.
Britton is poised to do all that and more as assistant director of the Gateway to Innovation (G2i), the district’s in-progress transformation of the former Pickens Middle School into a hub combining project-based learning, makerspaces, career pathways and workforce development for students ranging from third grade to high school.
Britton is excited about this new role as G2i prepares to open in January 2027, seeing it as a culmination of her experience thus far and a natural next step in her career.
“I have always been passionate about making learning engaging and meaningful, and the best way to do that is to connect education to real-world application,” Britton said. “I think [G2i] will create experiences that help students understand why learning matters.”
Britton began her professional career in 2014 as a special education teacher at Plain Elementary School in Greenville County. She transitioned to a second-grade teacher and was recognized as the county’s Emerging Teacher of the Year in 2018.
During this time, she earned both a master’s in educational leadership and began pursuing a master’s in instructional design and learning technology from Anderson University. In 2021, she assumed her most recent role as an instructional technology coach in the School District of Pickens County.
She served students and teachers throughout the district, supporting more than 70 classrooms in integrating effective instructional technology that develops the skills of 21st-century learners. She also became heavily involved in the district’s mobile learning lab, which traveled to schools to deliver STEM experiences, reaching approximately 6,000 students each year through coding, robotics and STEM programming.
However, despite a career that has taken her out of a special education classroom, Britton is still driven by the values instilled in her as an undergraduate at Clemson.
“Creating educational experiences that apply to and include all learners informed my instructional philosophy early on, and that has never changed,” Britton said. “Even though I have now learned to take a broader view, I think that learner-centered approach will guide me.”
Her third, most recent Clemson degree was an EdD in systems improvement science, a program she completed alongside a cohort of other district leaders from Pickens. Its focus on systems thinking and sustainable change strategies certainly pushed Britton to think in a “broader” way, but she also enjoyed the program because it required connecting learning to real-world practice.
The program requires participants to focus on a “problem of practice” in their own work setting that can be solved through research. Britton focused on instructional technology, professional development and technology integration in the district to ensure meaningful use of technology rather than merely increasing use.
“Activities such as screen-free coding and robotics activities help students learn how to think instead of simply how to use a device,” Britton said. “There’s a big difference there. I advocate for balanced technology use where technology is a tool for creation and problem solving rather than a tool for consumption.”
Britton was drawn to the position at G2i because it was designed to serve the broader Pickens community via elementary STEM programming and high school career and technical education pathways. That “balanced” approach to technology will be present, and no matter what grade level is served, it will be used to provide education that links to a practical use.
G2i also includes affordable, high-quality childcare for district employees — a major bonus for Britton, who is the mother of two young children, and other teachers, to encourage recruitment and retention in the district. If she takes a broad view now, it’s of the community where she has chosen to raise a family, and how she can play a part in making it the best it can be for them.
“Our goal is really to make great people in Pickens County, and we want to make the community a place they want to stay in,” Britton said. “I am really excited to be [at G2i] when we open our doors, because it’s truly going to be a place that helps students discover where they want to go and then helps them get there.”

MD Sass , a boutique asset management firm, published its second-quarter investor update for its flagship, the "MD Sass Concentrated Value Strategy." The letter can be downloaded here . In the first half of 2026, AI infrastructure stocks led the market, with the Russell 1000 Value increasing by 16.3%, outpacing the S&P 500 (10.2%) and Russell 1000 Growth (5.3%). This growth was fueled by semiconductor, memory, and hardware companies benefiting from AI development, even though they are considered cyclical. These sectors, representing only 7.7% of the Russell 1000 Value at the start of the year, contributed nearly 70% of its returns. The portfolio gained 10.0% in the second quarter, net of fees, compared to 13.9% for the Russell 1000 Value Index. Year-to-date, the strategy returned 6.6%, net of fees, versus 16.3% for the Index. The portfolio faced challenges due to limited exposure to companies with the greatest upside from AI infrastructure investments. It also lacked exposure to the Energy sector, which returned about 20% in the first half amid geopolitical tensions with Iran that increased commodity prices, affecting performance. The firm recognizes the importance of adapting its strategies while maintaining core investment principles as it explores future opportunities in emerging technological themes. Also, check the fund's top five holdings to see its best picks in 2026.

In its second-quarter 2026 investor letter, MD Sass Concentrated Value Strategy highlighted Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU ). Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), a leading semiconductor company manufacturing memory and storage products, contributed to the fund's performance this quarter. On August 28, 2026, Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) closed at $932.86 per share. The one-month return of Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) was 14.00%, and its shares gained 694.60% over the past 52 weeks. Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) has a market capitalization of $1.05 trillion.

MD Sass Concentrated Value Strategy stated the following regarding Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) in its Q2 2026 investor letter:

"We owned Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) for only a portion of the second quarter, but its impact was significant, as the stock appreciated approximately 50% during our holding period. Although MU had already experienced a massive run before we initiated our investment, most of the share price appreciation was driven by positive earnings revisions rather than multiple expansion. In fact, with the stock trading at approximately 6x our earnings estimate for the next 12 months, the market clearly signaled that MU was overearning and that a significant decline in earnings was imminent. We believed this assumption, although consistent with previous memory boom and bust cycles, was erroneous. We believed this cycle would remain stronger for much longer for three primary reasons. First, high bandwidth memory ("HBM") is growing rapidly, is less commodity oriented, and requires significantly more wafer capacity than traditional DRAM. Second, MU has established firm, multiyear supply agreements that provide unusually strong visibility and downside protection. Third, industry supply growth appears insufficient to accommodate the rapid increase in memory demand created by inference and agentic AI applications, which require substantial memory capacity and bandwidth. We sold our position during the first week of Q3 after both Micron and Sandisk (SNDK) shifted from the Russell 1000 Value Index to the Russell 1000 Growth Index as part of the late June reconstitution. We want the vast majority of CV's investments to be in companies represented in our benchmark and therefore decided to sell MU while retaining a small position in SNDK, which we purchased late in the quarter."

It also lacked exposure to the Energy sector, which returned about 20% in the first half amid geopolitical tensions with Iran that increased commodity prices, affecting performance. In its second-quarter 2026 investor letter, MD Sass Concentrated Value Strategy highlighted Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU). Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), a leading semiconductor company manufacturing memory and storage products, contributed to the fund's performance this quarter. On August 28, 2026, Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) closed at $932.86 per share. The one-month return of Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) was 14.00%, and its shares gained 694.60% over the past 52 weeks. Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) has a market capitalization of $1.05 trillion.

MD Sass Concentrated Value Strategy stated the following regarding Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) in its Q2 2026 investor letter:

"We owned Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) for only a portion of the second quarter, but its impact was significant, as the stock appreciated approximately 50% during our holding period. Although MU had already experienced a massive run before we initiated our investment, most of the share price appreciation was driven by positive earnings revisions rather than multiple expansion. In fact, with the stock trading at approximately 6x our earnings estimate for the next 12 months, the market clearly signaled that MU was overearning and that a significant decline in earnings was imminent. We believed this assumption, although consistent with previous memory boom and bust cycles, was erroneous. We believed this cycle would remain stronger for much longer for three primary reasons. First, high bandwidth memory ("HBM") is growing rapidly, is less commodity oriented, and requires significantly more wafer capacity than traditional DRAM. Second, MU has established firm, multiyear supply agreements that provide unusually strong visibility and downside protection. Third, industry supply growth appears insufficient to accommodate the rapid increase in memory demand created by inference and agentic AI applications, which require substantial memory capacity and bandwidth. We sold our position during the first week of Q3 after both Micron and Sandisk (SNDK) shifted from the Russell 1000 Value Index to the Russell 1000 Growth Index as part of the late June reconstitution. We want the vast majority of CV's investments to be in companies represented in our benchmark and therefore decided to sell MU while retaining a small position in SNDK, which we purchased late in the quarter."

Commentary: Sometimes the best classroom technology is no technology

Published 7:42 am Monday, August 31, 2026

By The Chicago Tribune Editorial Board/TNS

If a muscle atrophies, our bodies weaken. We can’t walk very far, we can’t lift things.

When your ability to think atrophies, well, that’s arguably a whole lot worse. “Cogito, ergo sum,” or — “I think, therefore I am,” as René Descartes put it.

Thinking, thus, is as elemental as breathing. Universities should create the conditions for students to learn how to do it well, and the University of Chicago has struck an important blow to that end.

Leaning on the convenience of artificial intelligence for writing assignments comes at a cognitive cost: A reduction in critical thinking, according to a 2025 study from researchers at MIT, Wellesley and the Massachusetts College of Art and Design.

A new policy for the U. of C.’s social sciences core aims to return the classroom to an analog experience in which students must generally read, write and analyze without AI’s assistance.

“At UChicago, we train students to use both reason and specialized knowledge in preparation for life as a free person,” the memo from Social Sciences Collegiate Division Master Jenny Trinitapoli reads. “… we first equip students to read, write, and think without dependence on AI, just as we equip students to read, write, and think beyond the bounds of conventional views or leading ideologies.”

In other words, this is about challenging students to think for themselves before introducing the life-altering capabilities of artificial intelligence into the equation.

Note, this memo is explicitly not anti-AI. Trinitapoli notes that technology can be “used for good scholarly purposes in other parts of the curriculum.”

It simply recognizes the proper sequence of things — think first, leverage tools after.

The same restraint applies to professors, who will not be permitted to employ AI to write syllabuses or course materials. AI use in grading is also tightly restricted.

This effort to cultivate our own minds, as Trinitapoli puts it, is noble and worthwhile, and absolutely in keeping with the university’s long and hallowed reputation as an institution where rigorous instruction and deep intellectual engagement are considered table stakes.

Notably, this policy does not apply to the whole school but to a set of discussion-based social science courses. U. of C. President Paul Alivisatos has made his broader philosophy known, too, and it comes across as entirely sensible, acknowledging the powerful assistance AI can offer when, say, doing data analysis while at the same time reinforcing the need for independent thought.

“The University has a duty of care to ensure that the education offered to you is responsive to these technological developments by teaching you how to think with machines, how to think without them, and how to think about them,” Alivisatos said in a June statement.

The U. of C. is not alone in reckoning with how to lasso AI in academic settings. Duke University earlier this month updated its AI guidance, reinforcing that students are expected to do their own work, unless authorized, and sharing the expectation that professors should come up with guidance on the use of AI in the classroom to be included in their syllabuses. All while firmly supporting AI literacy.

Columbia University, too, “embraces generative AI tools” while also demanding its students rely on the use of their own critical thinking skills in the pursuit of their education, meaning students are expected to do their assignments and exams without AI assistance, unless expressly permitted.

These universities are among our nation’s top schools, and what they do resonates far beyond the confines of campus. We expect others will follow suit.

We applaud the University of Chicago for recognizing the fundamental importance of teaching students to think for themselves.

articles.summary: A post-earnings drop handed one investor a reason to buy more Marvell Technology, not sell it, and a Google warrant that binds a hyperscaler to shareholder returns is only part of why he keeps hitting the buy button.
articles.content:

- NVDA +1.04%

- GOOG -2.34%

- AVGO +0.38%

Quick Read

- Marvell's Data Center revenue hit $2.17 billion, up 46% year over year, with management guiding roughly 50% growth in fiscal 2028.

Marvell's Data Center revenue hit $2.17 billion, up 46% year over year, with management guiding roughly 50% growth in fiscal 2028.

- Marvell offers purer AI data center exposure than NVIDIA or Broadcom, with Google holding a warrant for up to 7% of shares tied to revenue milestones.

Marvell offers purer AI data center exposure than NVIDIA or Broadcom, with Google holding a warrant for up to 7% of shares tied to revenue milestones.

- Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 37% and cash surged 221% to $3.93 billion, funding $200 million in quarterly stock buybacks with minimal debt pressure.

Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 37% and cash surged 221% to $3.93 billion, funding $200 million in quarterly stock buybacks with minimal debt pressure.

- Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Marvell Technology didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today .

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Marvell Technology didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today .

I keep hitting the buy button on Marvell Technology ( NASDAQ:MRVL ), and last Thursday's post-earnings drop of -10.28% gave me another window to add. I own this stock because it sits at the intersection of two irreversible build-outs: custom AI accelerators and the optical fabric connecting them. Every quarter the numbers validate why I refuse to trim.

Data Center Numbers That Keep Pulling Me Back

Data Center revenue hit $2.1715 billion in Q2 FY27, up 46% year over year, and now sits at 79% of total revenue versus 74% a year earlier. Total revenue landed at $2.739 billion, up 36.55%. Management sees fiscal 2027 revenue growing about 45% to roughly $12 billion and fiscal 2028 revenue growing about 50% year over year. CEO Matt Murphy said "AI-related bookings remain exceptionally robust". When a company raises the outlook on a business already growing this fast, I add.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Marvell Technology didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today .

Google Warrant Changes the Math

Marvell disclosed an expanded custom silicon agreement with Google that includes a warrant allowing Google to acquire up to 7% of Marvell's shares tied to revenue milestones. A hyperscaler is formally aligning its economics with mine. Custom revenue is expected to more than double year over year in fiscal 2028, and one analyst on the call framed the deal as $120 billion in cumulative revenue over six years at full milestone achievement, a scale Murphy did not push back on. The Celestial AI photonic fabric technology adds to the same story, and the whole trade sits inside a broader data-center buildout we mapped out in a free report on seven non-chipmaker AI infrastructure suppliers.

Margins, Cash, and Buybacks

Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 36.6% from 34.8%, with management guiding into the 38% to 40% long-term range by Q4. Cash sits at $3.93 billion, up 221.2% year over year. The company repurchased $200 million of stock in Q2, on top of $2.04 billion across FY26. Operating cash flow of $605.5 million funds the buyback machine, and net debt to EBITDA of 0.27 times shows the $4.963 billion long-term debt load is manageable.

Why Not Reach for NVIDIA or Broadcom Instead

The two names I could buy instead are NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) and Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ). Both are excellent businesses. Marvell offers what I want: a concentrated position where 79% of revenue already flows from the data center and a hyperscaler holds a warrant on up to 7% of the shares. Marvell's forward P/E of 60 pairs with data center growth of 46% year over year and a custom business expected to more than double next year. That is the pure-play exposure I want.

Risk I Refuse to Hand-Wave

Customer concentration is real. A handful of hyperscalers drive the bulk of growth, and any could pull volume in-house or shift to a rival. Add trade restrictions on Chinese customers and tariff uncertainty, and the concentration cuts both ways. What keeps me buying is that the Google warrant structurally binds the biggest concentration risk to my side of the table, and demand is broad-based across interconnect, switching, custom silicon, optical DSPs, and CXL memory expansion.

What Keeps My Buy Button Active

Shares are down 8.61% over the past week and still up 155.27% year to date at $216.62. With the Investor Day on October 6, 2026 set to detail custom revenue through fiscal 2029, I would rather be early than clever. I keep buying Marvell because the customer, the technology, and the balance sheet are all pointed the same direction, and the market handed me another discount to prove it.

articles.content:
News Details
Credo's Toucan PCIe® Retimer Achieves PCI Express® Compliance and Joins PCI Express® 6.x Integrators List
SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd (Credo) (NASDAQ: CRDO), an innovator in providing connectivity at scale through fast, reliable, and energy-efficient system solutions, today announced that its Toucan Gen6x16 PCI Express® (PCIe®) retimer has successfully achieved PCI-SIG® 6.x retimer compliance at 64.0 GT/s and is now listed on the PCI-SIG Integrators List.
Credo's Toucan Gen6x16 PCI Express® (PCIe®) retimer has successfully achieved PCI-SIG® 6.x retimer compliance at 64.0 GT/s and is now listed on the PCI-SIG Integrators List.
Key points:
- Credo's Toucan Gen6x16 PCIe retimer successfully completed PCI-SIG 6.x retimer compliance testing at the recent PCI-SIG Compliance Workshop which concluded on July 31.
- Toucan is now listed on the PCI-SIG Integrators List, giving customers added confidence in standards-based PCIe 6.0 deployment.
- The compliance milestone validates Toucan across electrical compliance, interoperability, and expanded PCIe 6.0 retimer protocol requirements.
- Toucan combines PCIe 6.0 performance with DSP-based SerDes, low-power operation and deep diagnostics through PILOT software.
Purpose-Built for Next-Gen Platforms
Toucan retimers address integration challenges in AI, HPC, and accelerated compute environments with:
- PCIe 6.0 technology-compatible interoperability
- Low-power design for dense accelerator platforms
- Advanced debug and diagnostics through award-winning PILOT tool
- Architecture aligned with PCIe 7.0 technology roadmaps
“As AI infrastructure scales from individual servers to rack-scale and cluster-scale architectures, the role of PCIe architecture connectivity becomes increasingly important," said Vishal Shah, Vice President of Product at Credo. “Achieving PCIe 6.0 specification compliance and inclusion on the PCI-SIG Integrators List validates the ability of Credo’s PCIe retimer to deliver the signal integrity, interoperability, diagnostics, and power efficiency required by next-generation AI systems. This milestone gives customers confidence that Toucan is ready for production deployment in the most demanding accelerated computing environments.”
“We congratulate Credo on achieving PCI-SIG 6.x compliance for its Toucan retimers,” said Al Yanes, PCI-SIG President and Chairperson. “Industry collaboration and adherence to open standards are essential to advancing the PCI Express technology ecosystem.”
Key Customer Benefits
- PCIe 6.0 specification x16 readiness for AI, HPC, cloud, and accelerated compute platforms.
- Reduced integration and qualification risk through standards-based validation.
- Faster platform bring-up and root-cause debug using PILOT diagnostics and telemetry.
- Reliable operation across complex high-speed topologies and high-loss channels.
- Low-power design for dense accelerator and server environments.
The successful completion of PCI-SIG 6.x retimer testing underscores Credo's continued execution in high-speed connectivity and reinforces Toucan as a key building block for reliable PCIe 6.0 technology deployment in modern AI infrastructure.
To learn more about Credo’s PCIe retimer solutions, visit https://credosemi.com/products/pcie/.
About Credo
Credo’s mission is to transform connectivity at scale through fast, reliable, and energy-efficient system solutions. Our high-speed copper and optical interconnect technologies deliver industry-leading power and performance from chip to cluster to meet the ever-expanding data infrastructure demands of AI.
Our vertically integrated connectivity portfolio is comprised of our flagship purple ZeroFlap (ZF) Active Electrical Cables (AECs) and ZF optical transceivers; optical components including silicon photonics-based photonic integrated circuits (SiPho PICs) and DSPs; OmniConnect AI memory and chip-to-chip interconnect; and retimers for Ethernet and PCIe—supported by our PILOT diagnostic and analytics software platform. Credo innovations enable our customers to connect the systems that connect the world.
For more information, please visit https://www.credosemi.com. Follow Credo on LinkedIn.
About PCI-SIG
PCI-SIG is the consortium that owns and manages PCI specifications as open industry standards. The organization defines industry standard I/O (input/output) specifications consistent with the needs of its members. Currently, PCI-SIG is comprised of over 1,000 companies. To join PCI-SIG, and for a list of the Board of Directors, visit https://www.pcisig.com/.

articles.title: Diffraqtion raises funding for quantum imaging technology
articles.description: Diffraqtion raises funding for quantum imaging technology SpaceNews
articles.description_html: Diffraqtion raises funding for quantum imaging technology  SpaceNews
articles.article_title: Diffraqtion raises funding for quantum imaging technology
articles.heading: Diffraqtion raises funding for quantum imaging technology
articles.summary: A startup has raised $10 million to advance technology for space cameras that promises to resolve details not possible with conventional systems.
articles.content:
WASHINGTON — A startup has raised $10 million from investors that include Lockheed Martin and Sumitomo to advance technology for space cameras that promises to resolve details not possible with conventional systems.
Diffraqtion announced Aug. 31 it closed a pre-seed round involving Lockheed Martin Ventures and Presidio Ventures, the venture arm of Sumitomo Corp., among other investors. The company said strong interest led it to cap the pre-seed round.
The company, based in Somerville, Massachusetts, and spun out of work done at the University of Maryland and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, is developing quantum cameras it says can get around the resolution limit of conventional cameras, known as the diffraction limit. That limit is a function of the wavelength of light and the diameter of the imager: To improve the resolution, one must use shorter wavelengths or larger apertures.
The diffraction limit “is just a limit that is imposed by the technique of direct imaging,” said Johannes Galatsanos, co-founder and chief executive of Diffraqtion, in an interview. “For a very long time, we have thought this is the limit.”
The company says it has developed a way to extract quantum information from photons using an approach called modal imaging. Another company co-founder, Saikat Guha, has worked on this technology for more than a decade.
“Instead of looking at intensity of the light, you’re looking at the shapes or the modes,” Galatsanos said. “When you’re looking at the shape of the light that comes to you, you can extract properties about the object that sent that light.”
An example he gave was taking an image of a satellite. While a conventional image might show only a blur, the company’s quantum imaging techniques could reveal the shape or orientation of the spacecraft. Simulations indicate the technology could resolve features 20 times smaller than conventional cameras.
The company has tested the technology in the lab and, in January, announced a $1.5 million Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Small Business Innovation Research contract to test the technology on ground-based telescopes.
Galatsanos said the pre-seed round will allow the company to develop its first full camera system with “much higher” performance than the one used in the lab and test it on telescopes. The company is also proposing to fly a version of the camera as a hosted payload on a spacecraft in 2028, but he said the company will need to raise additional funding for that milestone.
Initial interest in Diffraqtion’s technology is its use in space domain awareness. “You can say that this is a certain type of a satellite, or this is a satellite in a certain orientation, or this is a satellite versus debris or something else,” he said.
A downside of this technology, he acknowledged, is that while the sensor can return information about the shape of the object, it does not provide an image. The technology is best used in a “sensor fusion” approach that combines the shape information it provides with data from other cameras that can produce conventional images. “We always foresee this to be used in tandem with other sensors,” he said.
Since receiving the DARPA award in January, Diffraqtion has received inquiries about its sensor technology in a wide range of applications. That is one reason Sumitomo’s venture arm invested in the company. “They see the wider applications of this across robotics, drones and industrial inspections,” he said.
“What drew us to Diffraqtion is that the same physics advantage applies whether the camera is observing the sky or the Earth, or guiding a physical system,” said Ross Leav, senior vice president at Presidio Ventures, in a statement. “We see significant opportunity to bring this capability to industrial and commercial markets globally.”
“We invest in technologies with the potential to shape future mission capabilities,” said Chris Moran, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Ventures, in the statement. “This team’s rapid progress from laboratory development toward flight demonstration is particularly promising.”

articles.summary: AI changes the math of technology, so companies need to measure business value — not just track what they spend.
articles.content:

- Decision quality improvement
- Time-to-market acceleration
- Innovation capacity

Increasingly, technology is the business.

Many organizations are deploying AI rapidly without understanding:
- Long-term infrastructure costs
- Model maintenance costs
- Data quality costs
- Governance costs
- Security costs
- Regulatory costs
A technology economist examines the total lifecycle economics.
The cheapest AI solution today may become the most expensive solution over the next decade.

The central challenge of the AI era is no longer “Can we build it?”
The challenge is, “Should we build it, where should we deploy it, what value will it create, what risks will it introduce and what is the optimal economic allocation of technology capital?”

That is the domain of technology economics.
